_readme: Answers for the Ask Isaac chat on the tennis page. Each topic has an id, 'covers' (what questions it answers — this is what Jev reads to pick it), the answer shown to the visitor, and optional buttons. 'answer_parent' (optional) is shown instead when the visitor is asking for their child. 'next' is up to three follow-up questions shown as tappable chips after the answer; phrase them as a visitor would. Button types: book (private | half | semi | hitting; half is the 30-minute private lesson), email (subject), link (href), scroll (#section), open (a popup's id, e.g. clinicList or giftForm). A tip topic's 'title' is its heading on the practice tips page (/tips/), which the build makes from these answers. 'misuse' is what the chat says to abuse or attempts to give it instructions; 'personal' is prefixed when someone types contact details. A topic with an 'area' is a general tennis answer (rules, gear, technique...): the Worker first picks among Isaac's own topics and one option per entry in 'areas', then, when an area wins, among that area's topics; a new general answer needs an existing area. Edit freely; keep every fact true to the page. If nothing fits a question, the chat shows 'fallback'. After editing, run node tools/i18n/build.mjs and update the translated answers it lists.
greeting: Hi! These are my answers to what people ask most. Try prices, where I coach, who I teach, booking, or something in your game you want to fix.
fallback: I don't have that written down here. Email me and I'll answer you directly.
unavailable: The chat isn't answering right now. Email me and I'll get back to you.
misuse: I can only answer questions about lessons here.
personal: Please leave out phone numbers, addresses, schools and full names here. Email me for anything personal.

areas.covers: A question about the rules of tennis or how scoring works: points, games, sets, tiebreaks, deuce and advantage, serving rules, faults and foot faults, lets, whether a ball on the line is in, touching the net, or changing ends.

Etiquette and where or when to play: sportsmanship and court manners, calling lines in a friendly match, court surfaces (hard, clay, grass), playing in wind, sun, heat or at night, finding people to play with, or how leagues and tournaments work.

How to hit groundstrokes: forehand and backhand technique, grips, topspin, slice, flat shots, contact point, follow-through, lobs, drop shots, passing and approach shots, or footwork, the split step, the ready position and moving around the court.

How to serve, return serve or play at the net: serve grip, stance, toss, motion, flat, slice and kick serves, second serves, returning serve, volleys, half volleys, overheads and smashes, or when to come in.

Tactics and strategy in singles or doubles: shot selection, where to aim, patterns of play, playing a particular kind of opponent, court positioning, doubles formations, poaching, or working with a doubles partner.
The mental side of tennis: nerves, confidence, focus, anger or frustration, choking on big points, routines between points, bouncing back from mistakes, or handling a difficult opponent.

Tennis equipment in general: choosing or buying a racket, head size, weight, strings and string tension, restringing, grip size, overgrips, dampeners, tennis shoes, tennis balls, bags, clothing or accessories.

Fitness and health for tennis: warming up, stretching, cooling down, conditioning, speed and agility, strength training, hydration and heat, recovery, soreness, common aches and pains, or preventing injuries.

How to learn and get better at tennis in general: how to practise, drills, hitting against a wall, ball machines, how often to play, how long improving takes, starting as an adult, ratings like NTRP or UTR, plateaus, or how juniors develop.

Tennis words and the wider game: what a tennis term means, pro tennis, Grand Slams and tournaments, rankings, tennis history, why scoring goes 15-30-40, watching tennis, or how tennis compares with pickleball, padel or other sports.

topics.title: My serve goes into the net
topics.covers: The visitor's serve keeps going into the net, or their serve is too low.
topics.answer: A serve in the net usually means the toss is too low or too far in front, so you hit down on the ball too early. Toss a little higher, just in front of your hitting shoulder, and reach up to hit it at full stretch. Practise ten tosses without swinging: each one should come down in the same spot, in front of your front foot.

topics.title: My serve goes long
topics.covers: The visitor's serve goes long, past the service line, or out.
topics.answer: A long serve usually comes from a toss drifting behind you, which opens the racket face at contact. Keep the toss slightly in front, hit up and over the ball, and let the racket turn over after contact. Aim for the middle of the box, not the lines.

topics.title: I double fault a lot
topics.covers: The visitor double faults a lot, their second serve is weak or unreliable, or they get nervous on second serves.
topics.answer: Most double faults come from hitting the second serve like a slower first serve. A second serve needs more spin, not less speed: brush up the back of the ball so it clears the net with room and dips into the box. Practise a basket of second serves only, and count how many land in.

topics.title: My forehand goes into the net
topics.covers: The visitor's forehand goes into the net, or their groundstrokes are too low.
topics.answer: Forehands into the net usually mean the swing is too flat or the contact is late. Start the racket below the ball and finish high over your opposite shoulder, and meet the ball out in front of your body. Aim about three feet above the net: that height is your margin.

topics.title: My forehand flies long
topics.covers: The visitor's forehand flies long, sails out the back, or has no control.
topics.answer: A forehand that sails long is usually hit flat with an open racket face. Brush up the back of the ball for topspin, so it dips down into the court, and finish the swing over your shoulder instead of straight at the target. Aim deep to the middle, a few feet inside the baseline.

topics.title: My backhand is weak
topics.covers: The visitor's backhand is weak or inconsistent, or they avoid hitting backhands.
topics.answer: A weak backhand usually starts with a late turn. As soon as you see the ball coming to that side, turn your shoulders so your back is partly to the net, then swing from low to high out in front. Rally backhand to backhand cross-court with a partner until it feels routine.

topics.covers: The visitor can't keep a rally going, makes too many unforced errors, or wants more consistency.
topics.answer: Rallies end early when every shot aims too close to the lines or the net. Aim higher over the net and deep to the middle of the court, and count your rallies: try to beat your own record, not your partner. Consistency comes before power.

topics.covers: The visitor is late to the ball, feels rushed or jammed, or wants better footwork or movement.

topics.title: My elbow hurts (tennis elbow)
topics.covers: The visitor's elbow or forearm hurts when they play, or they ask about tennis elbow: what causes it, how to avoid it, or how to get rid of it.
topics.answer: Tennis elbow is a sore spot on the outside of the elbow, where the muscles that lift the wrist attach to the bone. On court it usually comes from a late, wristy backhand: the ball meets the racket beside you instead of in front, the wrist bends, and the forearm takes a jolt it isn't built for. Meet the ball out in front with a firm wrist and let the shoulders do the swinging, loosen your grip, and try softer strings or a bigger grip. Rest it while it's sore, and if it still hurts after a couple of weeks, see a doctor.

topics.covers: A parent asks how their child can practise at home, get started, or stay interested in tennis.
topics.answer: Keep it short and playful: catching and throwing, bouncing a ball on the racket, rallying over a line on the driveway with a soft ball. A few minutes several times a week builds more than one long session. In lessons, young beginners use slower, softer balls, so they rally sooner.

topics.title: I want to hit harder
topics.covers: The visitor wants more power, to hit harder or faster, or says their shots have no pace.
topics.answer: Power comes from the legs and the turn of your body, not the arm. Load your weight on the back leg, turn your shoulders, and let the racket accelerate through the ball with a relaxed grip, meeting it out in front. Squeezing the grip and swinging harder slows the racket down. Hit clean first, then add speed a little at a time.

topics.title: My returns are weak
topics.covers: Return of serve: the visitor misses returns, can't handle fast or spinning serves, or wants a better return.
topics.answer: Against a fast serve there's no time for a full swing. Split-step just as the server hits, turn your shoulders, and use a short, compact backswing, meeting the ball out in front with a firm wrist. Aim deep to the middle: a return in play beats a missed winner. Practise with a partner serving from a step inside the baseline.

topics.covers: The visitor asks about basic tennis etiquette or the unwritten rules in general: how to behave on court, what is polite, or what not to do as a new player.
topics.answer: Most tennis etiquette comes down to not disturbing other people's points. Wait for a point to end before walking behind a court or asking for a ball, call the score clearly when you serve, and give the other player the benefit of the doubt on close calls. Be on time, keep your voice down, and shake hands or tap rackets at the end.

topics.covers: How to call lines in casual or self-refereed play: who calls which side, what to do when you're unsure if a ball was in, and how to signal that a ball is out.
topics.answer: Without an umpire, you call the balls on your side of the net and your opponent calls theirs. A ball touching any part of the line is in, and if you aren't sure, it's in: only call it out when you clearly saw space between the ball and the line. Call it right away, loud enough to hear, and raise a finger so there's no confusion.

topics.covers: What a player is allowed to do when they think an opponent's line call was wrong: asking about the call, who has the final say, and getting an official involved at a tournament.
topics.answer: In self-called tennis, the call on each side belongs to the player on that side, so you can politely ask 'Are you sure?' but you can't overrule it. If they say they weren't sure, the ball should count as good. At a tournament, if calls keep going against you, ask the tournament desk whether an official can watch your match.

topics.covers: The visitor asks about score-calling courtesy in a friendly match: saying the score loudly enough for the other side to hear, and the habit that stops players losing track mid-game.
topics.answer: The server should call out the score before each point, loud enough for the other side to hear, with the server's score first. It takes a second and stops most arguments before they start. If you lose track anyway, go back to the last score you both agree on and play on from there.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to get a ball back from a neighboring court, or how to send another court's ball back to them, without disturbing their play.
topics.answer: Wait until the players on the other court finish their point, then ask for the ball or walk over to get it, never in the middle of their rally. When their ball comes to you, send it back between points with a gentle roll or an easy hit to one of the players. If a stray ball rolls onto your court during a point, call a let right away and replay the point.

topics.covers: Walking behind or past a court where people are playing, getting to a far court, or when it is okay to cross.
topics.answer: Wait until a point is over before you walk behind or alongside a court where people are playing. Movement in the background is distracting, especially for a player serving or hitting toward you. Then walk through quickly, close to the fence, and save chatting with the players for a break in their play.

topics.covers: How to give balls back to your opponent or the server between points, or whether to hit balls over the net to them.
topics.answer: Send the balls to the server, since they're the one who needs them, and do it between points rather than while they're getting ready to serve. A gentle hit on one bounce or a roll along the ground to where they're standing is the polite way. Don't smack balls back hard or scatter them around the court.

topics.answer: A pre-match warm-up is for both of you, so hit the ball back toward your opponent at a comfortable pace rather than trying to hit winners. Rally from the baseline, take turns at the net for volleys and overheads, and each take practice serves before the first point. It usually lasts about five to ten minutes, and tournaments may set the time.

topics.answer: In casual play there's no rule, so it varies by group. Many groups take turns bringing a new can, and often whoever brought the balls takes them home. topics.answer: It's a common courtesy to raise a hand or say sorry when you win a point off the top of the net or a mishit off the frame. Nobody did anything wrong, so it's a friendly gesture, not an admission, and the point still counts. If your opponent gets the lucky one, a nod or 'nice' keeps things friendly.

topics.covers: Whether it is okay to hit the ball at an opponent at the net, aiming at a player's body, or what to do after hitting someone with the ball by accident.
topics.answer: Hitting toward a player at the net is legal and a normal tactic, but in friendly play aim low, at the feet or hip, never at the head. If you hit someone by accident, check they're okay and apologize. Against a beginner or a much weaker player standing close, it's kinder to place the ball away from them.

topics.covers: Talking, shouting, grunting, music or phone use on court, or how loud it's okay to be while people are playing nearby.
topics.answer: Keep the noise down while points are being played on your court or the one next to you. Talk with your partner between points, cheer good shots once the rally ends, and keep music off or in earbuds unless everyone around agrees. Grunting as you hit is generally fine, but loud shouts during the opponent's shot can distract them and aren't fair play.

topics.answer: Meet at the net, shake hands or tap rackets, and say 'good match' whether you won or lost. A good winner keeps the celebration short, and a good loser gives honest credit and saves the frustration for later. Then pick up the balls, take your things, and leave the court on time for the next group.

topics.answer: Rules for public courts vary, so look first for a posted sign about time limits or reservations. Where there's no sign, a common courtesy is to give up the court after about an hour, or at the end of a set, when people are waiting. topics.covers: The differences between tennis court surfaces in general: hard, clay and grass, and how each changes the speed and bounce of the ball.
topics.answer: The surface changes how fast the ball comes through and how high it bounces. Hard courts sit in the middle, with a true, medium bounce, and they're the most common surface in the US. Clay is slower with a higher bounce, which means longer rallies, while grass is fast and low, which rewards big serves and coming to the net.

topics.covers: Playing on hard courts specifically: what they are made of, why they are so common, how they play, and how they affect your body and shoes.
topics.answer: Hard courts are concrete or asphalt with an acrylic coating, and they're the most common courts in the US because they're easy to maintain and play much the same in most weather. The bounce is predictable, which makes them good for learning. They're harder on joints and shoe soles than clay, so wear proper tennis shoes and warm up well.

topics.covers: Playing on clay courts: how clay plays, sliding, the higher bounce, longer rallies, or switching from hard courts to clay.
topics.answer: Clay is a slower surface where the ball grips and bounces higher, so points last longer and patience and topspin pay off. Players slide into shots, which takes practice: let your feet slide only as you reach the ball, not while you're still running. Clay is gentler on joints than hard courts, and the ball leaves a mark that can help settle a close call.

topics.covers: Playing on grass courts: how grass plays, why the ball stays low, and why few recreational players get to play on it.
topics.answer: Grass is the fastest traditional surface: the ball skids and stays low, and bounces can be uneven where the grass wears. Big serves, slices and getting to the net work well, while long baseline rallies are harder. Grass courts take a lot of care, so few public parks have them and most recreational players learn on hard courts or clay.

topics.covers: Indoor versus outdoor tennis: how playing indoors feels different, the ceiling and lighting, and adjusting when switching between indoor and outdoor courts.
topics.answer: Indoor courts take away wind, sun and rain, so the ball does what you hit it to do, and timing often feels easier. The catches are a ceiling that limits high lobs, plus a backdrop and lighting that take some getting used to. When you go back outdoors, give yourself a few games to adjust to the conditions again.

topics.covers: Which court surface is best for a beginner to learn on, or whether the surface matters much when starting tennis.
topics.answer: For a beginner, the best surface is the one you can get to regularly, and in most of the US that's a hard court. Hard courts give a steady, predictable bounce, which helps while you learn timing. Clay is a good option too if you have it nearby, since it slows the ball down and is gentler on the joints. Early on, court time matters far more than the surface.

topics.covers: Playing tennis in the wind: adjusting your shots and footwork, serving or tossing in wind, and playing with or against the wind.
topics.answer: In wind, play safer: aim farther inside the lines, use more topspin, and keep your feet moving with small steps because the ball will move late. Hitting into the wind, you can swing a bit harder because the air slows the ball, while with the wind behind you, add spin so the ball doesn't sail long. On serve, toss a little lower so the wind has less time to push it around.

topics.covers: The sun in your eyes when serving, hitting overheads or tracking lobs, and handling a bright, sunny day on court.
topics.answer: A cap or visor and sunglasses help most when the sun is in your eyes. On serve, you can move your toss slightly to the side or shift along the baseline so you aren't looking straight into it. For a lob you lose in the sun, let it bounce first and then hit it. Players change ends during a set, so the sun usually bothers both sides equally.

topics.covers: How hot weather changes playing conditions: the ball flying faster, the best time of day to play in summer, and planning tennis on a hot day.
topics.answer: In hot weather the ball flies faster and bounces higher, so a bit more spin helps keep it in. Play early in the morning or in the evening when you can, use any shade at changeovers, and drink water before you feel thirsty. If you feel dizzy, faint or sick, stop and cool down in the shade right away. Confusion or collapse in the heat is an emergency, so call 911.

topics.answer: You can play in the cold, but the ball travels slower and bounces lower, so you'll need to bend your knees more and swing through it fully. Wear layers you can take off as you warm up, and take a longer warm-up than usual before hitting hard. Skip play if there's frost or ice on the court, since it makes the surface slippery.

topics.answer: Don't play on a wet court: hard courts get slippery, and the painted lines are the most slippery spots of all. Damp patches also make the ball skid and soak it, so it gets heavy. How fast a court dries depends on sun and wind, and some facilities use squeegees to clear puddles. If it starts to rain during a match, stop as soon as the lines get slick.

topics.answer: If you hear thunder, stop and get off the court right away: a tennis court is open ground surrounded by metal fencing. Head into a building or a hard-topped car, not under a tree or an open shelter. A common safety rule is to wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back out.

topics.answer: Playing under lights is common, but the ball can be harder to track, especially on lobs that rise past the lamps. Give your eyes a few minutes to adjust and focus on watching the ball a little longer before you swing. The air usually cools in the evening, so the ball may feel a bit slower. topics.answer: The easiest way is to go where players already are: clinics, round robins, leagues and ladders all put you with people near your level. Many areas also have community groups or apps for finding partners, and regulars at public courts are often happy to swap numbers. topics.answer: Wait until people finish a point or take a break, then ask simply whether they'd be up for a hit sometime, and mention your level so they know what to expect. Players in the middle of a match usually won't want to stop, so suggesting another day works better. topics.answer: A round robin or social mixer is a casual event where players rotate partners and opponents, usually in short doubles sets or timed games. You don't need to bring a partner, and it's one of the quickest ways to meet players near your level. Formats vary by host, so ask about the level and how the rotation works when you sign up.

topics.answer: Recreational leagues group players by level, and USTA leagues use NTRP ratings to do it. Teams play other teams across a season, and a team match is usually split into several singles and doubles matches, called lines: the team that wins more lines wins. Many use a single-elimination draw, sometimes with a consolation draw for early losers, while others use round-robin groups. topics.answer: Nerves before a match are normal and usually a sign you care, so aim to manage them rather than make them vanish. Keep the day simple: pack your bag the night before, arrive early, and follow the same warm-up every time. In the warm-up, focus on moving your feet and watching the ball, not on how well you're hitting. Most nerves fade after the first few points.

topics.answer: On big points, pick a shot you trust and commit to it rather than trying something new. Pressure makes muscles tense, so breathe out slowly before the point and relax your grip a little. Aim for bigger targets with good height over the net, and make your opponent earn the point. topics.answer: Leads slip when players start protecting them: hitting softer, playing safer than usual and hoping the opponent misses. Keep doing what got you ahead, with the same targets and the same pace. Think about the next point, not the score, and expect the other player to raise their level when they're behind. topics.answer: Confidence on court comes from evidence, so build it in practice with things you can count: rally streaks, serves in a row, games won in a practice set. Before matches, remind yourself of what you do well rather than what might go wrong. In a match, judge yourself on effort and decisions, which you control, not only on the result.

Give your eyes a job during points, like watching the ball right onto the strings, and use the gap between points to reset with a breath and a look at your racket. topics.answer: Anger usually costs you the next point too, so the goal is to let it out quickly and safely, then reset. Turn away from the court, take a slow breath, and use a small cue like adjusting your strings to mark the end of it. Never throw or smash a racket: it's unsafe and can get you penalized in matches. Turn your back, picture the shot you meant to hit, and tell yourself something useful, like 'more height' or 'watch the ball'. Then put your full attention on the next point. topics.answer: A short routine between points helps you let go of the last point and get ready for the next one. Turn away and walk back slowly, breathe out, touch your strings or towel, then decide on a simple plan, like a first-serve target or a deep return. Keep it brief and the same every time so you stay steady and don't hold up play.

topics.answer: A pre-serve routine gives your mind and body the same starting point every time, which matters most when you're nervous. Keep it simple: set your feet, decide where you're aiming, bounce the ball the same number of times, breathe out, then serve. topics.covers: Thinking too much about the score or the result during a match, worrying about winning or losing mid-match, or staying in the present one point at a time.
topics.answer: Thinking about the result pulls you out of the point you're actually playing. Bring your attention back to things happening now: your feet, the ball, your target for the next shot. Some players use a cue like touching the strings to mark a fresh start on every point. Winning comes from playing the current point well, again and again.

How do I stay focused?
What goals should I set?

topics.covers: A parent asks how to help a child who gets upset, cries or melts down when losing or making mistakes in tennis.
topics.answer: Kids get upset because they care, so stay calm yourself and keep the focus on effort and fun rather than the score. After a match, let them settle before talking, ask what they enjoyed, and praise things they control, like trying hard or being a good sport. Teach a simple reset for mistakes, such as a deep breath and a turn to the back fence. Your calm helps more than any advice.

What's the etiquette for watching a match?
Do you teach beginners?

topics.covers: How to become mentally tougher in tennis overall, or how to train and practise the mental side of the game.
topics.answer: Mental toughness is a set of habits you can practise like a stroke. Play practice points and sets with real scoring, start some games at 30-40 down to rehearse pressure, and use your match routine in practice too. Afterward, note how you handled the tough moments, not only how you hit. A hitting session where we play sets is a good place to train this.

topics.covers: Getting frustrated by bad luck: an opponent's net cords, mishits that win, bad bounces, or feeling like every break goes against you.
topics.answer: Lucky shots and bad bounces are out of your control and tend to even out, so give them a moment and move on. Over a whole match, the player who stays steady after unlucky points usually comes out ahead. A small reset, like a breath and a look at your strings, helps you let it go. Then focus on the next point, the only one you can change.

topics.covers: How to use changeovers and set breaks during a match to reset: what to think about, drinking and resting, and planning the next games.
topics.answer: Use changeovers to reset and plan: sit down, drink some water, and breathe slowly for the first part. Then ask yourself two quick questions: what's working, and what's one thing to change. Stand up with a clear plan for the next two games, such as more first serves in or playing to their weaker side. Leave the last games behind as you walk back out.
next: How do I come back when I'm losing?

How do I stay focused?

topics.covers: Body language on court: looking confident, not showing frustration to an opponent, and how posture affects how you feel and play.
topics.answer: Your body language affects both you and your opponent, so walk tall, keep your head up and move with purpose between points, even when things are going badly. Slumped shoulders and dropped rackets tell the other player you're struggling, and they can make you feel worse too. Act calm and ready, and your mind often follows.
next: How do I build confidence?

What should I do between points?

topics.covers: Setting goals for a match, practice or season: process goals versus outcome goals, and choosing what to focus on.
topics.answer: Set goals you control, called process goals, rather than only outcome goals like winning a match. Good examples are getting most first serves in, keeping three balls in play before attacking, or using your routine on every point. Pick one or two per match and check them honestly afterward. Outcome goals can still motivate you, but process goals are what get you there.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to choose or buy their first tennis racket as an adult beginner, or what kind of racket a beginner should get.
topics.answer: For a first adult racket, pick a light to medium weight frame with a head around 100 square inches and the standard 27-inch length. That combination is easy to swing and forgiving when you miss the center of the strings. Get the right grip size, and skip pro models for now: they are usually heavier and less forgiving.
next: What grip size do I need?
What head size should I get?
Can I try a racket before buying?

topics.covers: The visitor asks about racket head size: oversize versus midsize, square inches, or how head size affects power, control and the sweet spot.
topics.answer: For most beginners and intermediate players, a head of around 100 square inches is the sweet middle. Most adult rackets fall between about 95 and 110 square inches. A bigger head gives a larger sweet spot and more power, so off-center hits still go somewhere useful, while a smaller head gives more control and precision but asks for cleaner contact.
next: Should my racket be light or heavy?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether their racket should be light or heavy, or how racket weight affects power, control, stability and arm comfort.
topics.answer: Pick the heaviest racket you can swing comfortably for a whole session without your form slipping. A lighter racket is easier to swing and move around, which helps beginners and players with shorter strokes. A heavier racket is more stable, hits through the ball with less effort and passes less shock to your arm, but it tires you sooner.
next: What is racket balance?
What does racket stiffness mean?
How do I choose a racket?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what racket balance means: head-light, head-heavy or even balance, or the balance point of a racket.
topics.answer: Neither is better for everyone: balance is where a racket's weight sits along its length, and it changes how the racket swings. A head-heavy racket carries more weight toward the tip, which adds power and is common in light frames. A head-light racket keeps more weight in the handle, so it feels quicker for volleys and fast swings. Even balance sits in between, and the balance point is measured from the bottom of the handle.
next: Should my racket be light or heavy?
Are longer rackets better?
What head size should I get?

topics.covers: The visitor asks about racket length: the standard 27 inches, extended or longer rackets, or the maximum length allowed by the rules.
topics.answer: The standard adult racket is 27 inches long, and the rules allow up to 29 inches. Extended rackets, usually about half an inch to an inch longer, give extra reach and leverage on serves and groundstrokes, but they feel slightly slower to maneuver. Most players do best starting with the standard length.
next: What size racket for my child?
Should my racket be light or heavy?
How do I choose a racket?

topics.covers: A parent asks what size racket their child needs, junior racket sizes in inches, or when a child should move up to an adult racket.
topics.answer: Junior rackets come in lengths such as 19, 21, 23, 25 and 26 inches, and you choose by the child's height and reach rather than age alone. A quick check: with the child holding the racket by the grip, arm straight down by their side, the tip should sit just above the ground. Most juniors move to a full 27-inch racket once they can swing it without strain.
next: What are red, orange and green balls?
Do you teach beginners?
What grip size do I need?

topics.covers: The visitor asks about racket stiffness or flex, a stiff versus flexible frame, or how stiffness affects power, feel and arm comfort.
topics.answer: Stiffness describes how much the frame bends when it meets the ball. A stiffer frame returns more energy, so it feels powerful, but it also sends more shock into your arm. A more flexible frame feels softer and gives more feel and comfort, at the cost of some free power. If your arm gets tired or sore easily, lean toward a more flexible frame.
next: What strings should I use?
Should my racket be light or heavy?
Do dampeners help?

topics.covers: The visitor asks about string patterns such as 16x19 or 18x20, open versus dense patterns, and how they affect spin, control and string life.
topics.answer: The string pattern is the number of main and cross strings, such as 16x19 or 18x20. An open pattern like 16x19 has more space between strings, so it grips the ball for more spin and easier power, but the strings wear out sooner. A dense pattern like 18x20 gives a flatter, more controlled shot and longer string life. Most players do well with 16x19.

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether they need an expensive or professional-level racket, or whether to use the same racket a pro player uses.
topics.answer: No: the best racket is the one that suits your swing, not the one a pro uses. Pro frames are usually heavier, with smaller heads, and players at that level often customize them, so they can feel like hard work for most club players. A mid-range racket in the right weight and grip size will help your game far more.
next: How do I choose a racket?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether they can try or test a racket before buying it, about demo rackets, or how to compare rackets.
topics.answer: Yes: many tennis shops and clubs run demo programs that let you borrow a few rackets for a short time before you buy. Try them on the same day against the same partner, hit serves and volleys as well as groundstrokes, and notice which one you stop thinking about. That's usually the one.

Should I buy a used racket?
Do I need my own racket?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether to buy a used or secondhand racket, or what to check when buying one.
topics.answer: A used racket can be a good buy if the frame is sound. Check closely for cracks, especially around the top of the head and the throat, look for broken or missing grommets (the plastic tubes the strings pass through), and make sure the grip size fits you. Plan to restring it, since old strings lose their life even when they look fine.
next: When should I replace my racket?

topics.covers: The visitor asks when to replace their racket, whether rackets wear out, or what to do with a cracked or damaged frame.
topics.answer: Replace a racket when the frame cracks, because a cracked frame can't be reliably repaired and may break further. Without damage, a racket lasts for years: what wears out much sooner are the strings and the grip, so restring and regrip first if it starts to feel dead. Scuffed paint on the frame is only cosmetic.
next: How often should I restring?
How do I look after my racket?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to look after or protect a racket: storing it, bumper guards, scraping it on the court, or throwing it.
topics.answer: Keep your racket in a bag or cover, away from extreme heat and cold, and wipe the grip after you play. Try not to scrape it along the court when you pick up balls: the bumper guard on top of the frame protects it, but it wears through and can be replaced. And don't throw it or bang it on the ground, because that's the quickest way to crack a frame.
next: Can I leave my racket in the car?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether leaving a racket in a hot car or trunk damages it, or how heat and cold affect strings and frames.
topics.answer: It's best not to leave your racket in a hot car. Heat can make strings lose tension faster, and very high heat can harm the frame over time. If you must leave it in the car, keep it out of direct sun or in a bag with an insulated compartment, and take it inside with you once you're home.
next: How do I look after my racket?
How often should I restring?
What should I keep in my tennis bag?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what grip size they need, how to measure racket grip size, or what happens if the grip is too big or too small.
topics.answer: To find your grip size, hold the racket with a forehand grip and check whether the index finger of your other hand fits snugly in the gap between your fingertips and your palm. No gap means the grip is too small, and lots of room means it is too big. Adult sizes run from about 4 to 4 5/8 inches. If you're between sizes, go smaller and add an overgrip to build it up.
next: What is an overgrip?
How do I choose a racket?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what an overgrip is, why players use one, tacky versus dry overgrips, or how often to change an overgrip.
topics.answer: An overgrip is a thin wrap that goes over the racket's main grip. It adds a little cushioning and tack, soaks up sweat, and makes the handle slightly thicker. Tacky overgrips feel sticky, while dry ones suit players whose hands sweat a lot. Change it when it looks shiny, worn or slippery, which for frequent players can be every week or two.

How do I replace my grip?
What grip size do I need?

topics.covers: The visitor's racket slips in their hand because the grip is worn or their hands are sweaty or wet.
topics.answer: A slipping racket usually means the grip is worn or your hands are wet. Put on a fresh overgrip, try a dry-feel one if you sweat a lot, and wear wristbands to stop sweat running into your palm. Keep a towel by the fence and dry your hand between points. Once the grip isn't slick, you can hold the racket loosely without it moving.
next: What is an overgrip?

How do I replace my grip?

topics.covers: The visitor asks about replacing the racket's main or base grip, the difference between a replacement grip and an overgrip, or a worn or torn handle wrap.
topics.answer: The replacement grip is the thicker, cushioned wrap fitted directly on the handle, and an overgrip goes on top of it. Replace it when it's torn, hard, flattened or no longer comfortable, which is far less often than an overgrip. You can do it yourself: peel off the old one, start at the bottom of the handle, and wind the new one up with a slight overlap, keeping it tight.
next: What is an overgrip?
What grip size do I need?

topics.covers: The visitor asks about vibration dampeners: what they do, whether they help the arm, or where they are allowed on the strings.
topics.answer: A dampener is a small rubber piece that sits in the strings near the throat of the racket. It quiets the ping of the strings and changes the feel, but it does little to reduce the shock that reaches your arm. The rules allow it as long as it sits outside the area where the strings cross. Use one if you like the feel: it's purely a preference.
next: What does racket stiffness mean?
What strings should I use?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what kind of tennis strings to use, or the difference between natural gut, synthetic gut, multifilament, polyester and hybrid strings.
topics.answer: Most recreational players do well with synthetic gut or a multifilament string. Synthetic gut is a durable all-rounder, while multifilament is softer and easier on the arm. Polyester is stiff and favors spin and control for hard hitters, and natural gut, made from animal intestine, is the most elastic and comfortable but costs the most. A hybrid uses one type for the main strings and another for the crosses.
next: Are poly strings good for beginners?

What does string gauge mean?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether polyester (poly) strings are right for them or for beginners, or why advanced players use poly.
topics.answer: Polyester strings usually aren't the best choice for beginners. They are stiff, which gives hard hitters control and spin, but they feel harsh at slower swing speeds, pass more shock to the arm, and lose tension quickly even when they don't break. If you're still building your strokes, a softer synthetic gut or multifilament will feel better.

What tension should I string at?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what tension to string their racket at, or how higher or lower string tension affects power and control.
topics.answer: Start in the middle of the tension range printed on your racket, usually inside the throat or on the frame. Lower tension gives more power and a softer, more comfortable feel, while higher tension gives more control but less power. Many rackets recommend somewhere around 50 to 60 pounds. Change it a few pounds at a time and notice the difference.
next: How often should I restring?
What strings should I use?
What string pattern is best?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how often to restring a racket, how to tell when strings are worn out or dead, or whether strings lose tension without playing.
topics.answer: A common rule of thumb is to restring as many times a year as you play each week, so playing twice a week means restringing about twice a year. Strings lose tension over time even if they never break, so the ball starts to fly or feel dead. If your racket feels different from how it used to, or the strings keep sliding out of place, it's time.

topics.covers: The visitor broke a string, asks whether they can keep playing with a broken string, or whether one string can be replaced on its own.
topics.answer: Stop using the racket until it's restrung, because a broken string changes how the ball comes off and puts uneven stress on the frame. A stringer will replace the whole set of strings rather than just the broken one, which keeps the tension even. If you break strings often, try a thicker gauge or a more durable string.
next: What does string gauge mean?

What strings should I use?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what string gauge means, thick versus thin strings, or what numbers like 16 and 17 on string packets mean.
topics.answer: Gauge is a string's thickness, and a higher number means a thinner string, so 17 is thinner than 16. Thinner strings give a little more spin and feel but break sooner, while thicker strings last longer and feel slightly firmer. Gauges 16 and 17 are the most common, and 16 is a sensible starting point for most players.

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether they need tennis shoes, or whether running shoes, sneakers or cross-trainers are OK for playing tennis.
topics.answer: Tennis shoes are worth having, because tennis is full of quick side-to-side movement. They have firm sides, a flatter, stable sole and a tough toe for dragging. Running shoes are built for moving straight ahead on a soft, raised heel, which makes it easier to roll an ankle when you change direction. They'll do for a casual first hit, but switch once you play regularly.

topics.covers: The visitor asks about shoes for different court surfaces: hard court, clay court or grass court shoes, tread patterns, or non-marking soles.
topics.answer: The right shoe depends on the surface you play on most. Hard court shoes have a tough, durable sole for gritty courts, clay court shoes use a full zigzag (herringbone) tread that grips loose clay and sheds it as you move, and grass shoes have small rubber nubs. All-court shoes are a fine choice if you play on several surfaces. Whatever you buy, many courts require non-marking soles.

topics.covers: The visitor asks when to replace tennis shoes, how long tennis shoes last, or signs that shoes are worn out.
topics.answer: Replace tennis shoes when the tread is worn smooth, especially under the ball of the foot, or when the cushioning feels flat and the shoe no longer feels supportive. Frequent players often wear through a pair in a few months, while once-a-week players get much longer. Worn shoes grip less, so they make slips and rolled ankles more likely.

Do I need clay court shoes?
How do I prevent blisters?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how long tennis balls last, when balls go flat or dead, or whether an unopened can of balls goes bad.
topics.answer: Pressurized balls start losing pressure as soon as you open the can, so for casual play a can usually lasts a few sessions before the bounce feels flat. Squeeze a ball: if it gives easily or bounces low next to a new one, it's done for match play, though it can still be useful for practice. Sealed cans keep their pressure much longer, but not forever.

topics.covers: The visitor asks what pressureless tennis balls are, how they differ from regular pressurized balls, or whether they are good for practice.
topics.answer: Pressureless balls get their bounce from a thick rubber core instead of air pressure, so they don't go flat and last far longer than regular balls; the felt wears out first. They feel heavier and firmer off the strings. That makes them great for ball baskets, ball machines and wall practice, but most players prefer pressurized balls for matches.

What's extra duty felt?
How can I practise on my own?

topics.covers: The visitor asks about kinds of yellow tennis balls: extra duty versus regular duty felt, balls for hard courts versus clay, or high altitude balls.
topics.answer: Extra duty balls have a thicker, more durable felt made for hard courts, which wear felt down quickly, so they're the usual pick for outdoor hard courts. Regular duty balls have a thinner felt that picks up less clay, so they suit clay and indoor courts. There are also high altitude balls for courts well above sea level, where regular balls fly and bounce too much.

topics.covers: The visitor asks what kind of tennis bag to get, backpack versus racket bag, or what to keep stocked in a tennis bag for regular play (not what to bring to a lesson).
topics.answer: A backpack with a racket sleeve is enough for one or two rackets, and a bigger racket bag makes sense once you carry several. Either way, keep it stocked with water, a towel, a spare overgrip, balls, sunscreen, a hat, a snack, and some blister tape or bandages. An insulated compartment helps protect your strings from heat if the bag sits in a car.

topics.covers: The visitor asks what to wear to play tennis, about tennis clothing or moisture-wicking clothes, or about club dress codes.
topics.answer: Wear comfortable athletic clothes that let you move and stretch freely, ideally in a light, moisture-wicking fabric rather than cotton, which stays heavy when it's wet. Shorts or skirts with pockets, or a ball clip, make serving easier. Tennis shoes matter more than anything else you wear. Some clubs have dress codes, and a few still ask for white, so check before you play somewhere new.

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether they can or should wear sunglasses while playing tennis, or what kind of sunglasses to choose.
topics.answer: Yes, sunglasses are allowed, and many players wear them, especially when serving or hitting overheads into the sun. Choose sports glasses with impact-resistant lenses and a snug fit, so they stay put when you move and sweat. Some people find tinted lenses change how they judge the ball, so try them in practice before a match.

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether to wear a cap, hat, visor, headband or sweatband for tennis, cap versus visor in hot weather, or how to keep sweat out of their eyes.
topics.answer: A cap or visor is a good idea on bright days, because it keeps sun and sweat out of your eyes. A cap shades your whole head, while a visor lets heat escape from the top, so many players choose a visor when it's hot. Headbands and wristbands catch sweat before it reaches your eyes or your grip. Pick a light, breathable fabric.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to warm up their body before playing tennis, getting muscles and joints ready, or what a good warm-up routine looks like. Not the pre-match hit with an opponent (courts_warmup).
topics.answer: Spend 5 to 10 minutes getting warm before you hit hard. Start with light movement such as easy jogging, side shuffles and skipping, then add dynamic moves like leg swings, arm circles, lunges and trunk turns. On court, begin with gentle mini tennis near the service line, move back to the baseline, and hit a few easy serves before going full speed.

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether to stretch before playing, or the difference between static stretching and dynamic stretching.
topics.answer: Before playing, use dynamic stretches that move you through a range of motion, such as leg swings, walking lunges and arm circles. Long static holds, where you stretch and stay still, are better saved for after you play, since holding them right before hard effort can briefly reduce your power. Gentle static stretching afterward helps you cool down and keep your flexibility.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to cool down after playing tennis, or what to do right after a session or match.
topics.answer: Finish with a few minutes of easy movement, such as light hitting or walking, so your heart rate comes down gradually. Then do some gentle stretches for your calves, thighs, hips, shoulders and forearms, and drink water. If you played hard or in the heat, have a snack with some carbohydrate and protein within a couple of hours.

topics.covers: The visitor asks which stretches help tennis players, how long to hold a stretch, or how to improve flexibility.
topics.answer: The most useful stretches for tennis target the calves, hamstrings, quadriceps (the front of the thigh), hip flexors, glutes, shoulders and forearms. Hold each one gently for about 20 to 30 seconds, without bouncing, and breathe normally. You should feel a mild pull, never pain. Stretching a little most days improves flexibility more than one long session a week.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to get fit for tennis, what cardio or conditioning to do off court, or about interval training for tennis.
topics.answer: Train the way tennis is played: short, hard bursts with rest in between. Interval work such as 10 to 20 second shuttle runs or sprints, each followed by a rest, matches the rhythm of points. Add one or two longer, steady sessions a week, like jogging, cycling or swimming, to build a base. Build up gradually over several weeks rather than all at once.

topics.covers: The visitor gets tired, runs out of energy, gets out of breath or loses their legs late in long matches or long sessions.
topics.answer: Running out of energy late in a match usually comes from a mix of fitness, fuel and pacing. Eat a proper meal a few hours before, sip water at every changeover, and bring a snack for long matches. Use the time between points to breathe and reset instead of rushing. Off court, interval training builds the stamina to last, and it improves steadily with regular work.

topics.covers: The visitor asks for agility drills or ways to change direction faster, such as ladder drills, cone drills, side shuffles or jump rope.
topics.answer: Good agility drills for tennis include side shuffles, cone drills where you touch a cone and change direction, ladder footwork, and jump rope. On court, try sprinting from the middle of the baseline to touch each sideline and the service line in turn, coming back to the middle each time. Keep your steps quick and small, stay low, and rest fully between rounds so the quality stays high.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to get faster around the court through off-court training, or how to improve first-step quickness or reaction speed.
topics.answer: Speed on court is mostly about your first two or three steps, so train short bursts. Sprint 5 to 10 yards from different starting positions, have a friend point left or right for you to react to, and add skater jumps (bounding side to side) once your legs are strong. Keep each rep short and sharp with plenty of rest, because tired sprints teach slow habits.

topics.covers: The visitor asks what strength training or gym work helps tennis, or which exercises to do for legs, hips and upper body.
topics.answer: Two or three short strength sessions a week help both your tennis and injury prevention. Focus on the legs and hips (squats, lunges, step-ups), the upper back (rows), the core, and light band work for the shoulders. Start light, learn good form first, and add weight slowly. If you're new to lifting, a session or two with a qualified trainer is a good start.

topics.covers: The visitor asks about core exercises for tennis, or how to build trunk strength and rotation for their strokes.
topics.answer: Your core links your legs to your racket, so train it both to hold steady and to rotate. Good exercises are planks, side planks, glute bridges, dead bugs (lying on your back and slowly lowering an opposite arm and leg), and rotational throws with a light medicine ball against a wall. Do a few sets two or three times a week, keeping your lower back steady rather than arched.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to strengthen or protect their shoulder for serving, or about rotator cuff and resistance band exercises to prevent shoulder problems.
topics.answer: Light resistance band work two or three times a week helps protect a serving shoulder. Useful moves are external rotations (elbow tucked at your side, rotating the forearm outward against the band), rows, and squeezing your shoulder blades back and down. Keep the band light and the movement slow. Also warm up before serving, and build up the number of serves gradually.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to strengthen their wrists, forearms or grip for tennis.
topics.answer: A few simple exercises build forearm and grip strength: squeezing a soft ball, wrist curls and reverse wrist curls with a light dumbbell, and slowly turning a light weight palm up and palm down. Do a couple of sets a few times a week, keeping the weight light and the movement slow. Stronger forearms help, but a relaxed grip on court matters just as much.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how much water to drink when playing tennis, when to drink, or whether they need sports drinks or electrolytes.
topics.answer: Start the session well hydrated, then sip water at every changeover rather than waiting until you feel thirsty. For long sessions, heavy sweating or hot days, a sports drink or electrolyte tablet helps replace the salt you lose. Afterward, keep drinking until your urine is pale yellow. Needs vary a lot from person to person, so learn what works for you.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to play safely in hot weather, or about heat exhaustion, heat stroke, overheating or feeling dizzy from the heat while playing.
topics.answer: In the heat, play early or late in the day, drink before you're thirsty, and rest in the shade at changeovers with a cold towel on your neck. Stop at once if you feel dizzy, sick, weak, or get a headache or cramps: get into the shade, cool down, drink, and see a doctor if you don't feel better soon. If someone becomes confused, faints or has very hot skin, call emergency services right away.

topics.covers: The visitor gets muscle cramps while playing tennis, such as calf, thigh or hand cramps, and asks what to do or how to prevent them.
topics.answer: When a cramp hits, stop playing, gently stretch and massage the muscle until it relaxes, and drink fluids with some electrolytes. To prevent cramps, start well hydrated, keep drinking during play, eat properly beforehand, and build fitness gradually for longer matches. If cramps keep coming back, or the pain is sharp or lasts after the cramp eases, see a doctor or physical therapist.

topics.covers: The visitor asks what to eat before playing tennis, during long matches, or after playing.
topics.answer: Eat a balanced meal with plenty of carbohydrate two to three hours before you play, and if you need more, a light snack such as a banana or toast about an hour before. Avoid heavy, greasy food right before. During long matches, a banana or an energy bar at changeovers keeps you going. Afterward, have a meal with carbohydrate and protein to help you recover.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to recover after a hard match, tournament day or long session, or how to feel ready to play again.
topics.answer: Recovery comes down to fluids, food, sleep and gentle movement. After a hard session, rehydrate, eat a meal with carbohydrate and protein, and stretch lightly. Sleep matters most, so protect it. The next day, an easy walk, bike ride or light hit usually feels better than complete rest, and foam rolling can ease tight muscles.
next: Why am I sore after tennis?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether it's OK to play tennis every day, how many rest days they need, or about overtraining and overuse.
topics.answer: You can play often, but mix hard days with easy ones and give yourself at least one or two lighter or rest days a week. Overuse problems usually come from doing too much too soon, so increase your playing time gradually. If you feel run down or your play keeps getting worse, take a few days off. If something starts to hurt, stop, and see a doctor or physical therapist if the pain is sharp or lasts.

topics.covers: The visitor is sore or stiff the day after playing, asks whether muscle soreness after tennis is normal, or how to ease it.
topics.answer: Some muscle soreness a day or two after playing is normal, especially if you're new to tennis or played longer or harder than usual. It usually fades within a few days, and gentle movement, light stretching, fluids and sleep help. Soreness is different from pain: if you feel sharp pain, pain in a joint, swelling, or soreness that lasts, stop playing and see a doctor or physical therapist.

topics.covers: The visitor's wrist hurts or aches from playing tennis, or they ask about wrist pain.
topics.answer: If your wrist hurts, stop playing and rest it rather than playing through it. In tennis, wrist strain is often linked to meeting the ball late, flicking the wrist on topspin shots, or squeezing the grip too hard, so it's worth looking at your technique once it settles. If the pain is sharp, comes with swelling, or lasts more than a few days, see a doctor or physical therapist.

How do I avoid injuries?

topics.covers: The visitor's shoulder hurts, especially when serving or hitting overheads, or they ask about shoulder pain from tennis.
topics.answer: If your shoulder hurts, stop serving and rest it, because pushing through shoulder pain can make it worse. In tennis, shoulder strain often builds from hitting too many serves, serving mostly with the arm instead of the legs and body, or weak muscles around the shoulder blade. If the pain is sharp, wakes you at night, or lasts more than a few days, see a doctor or physical therapist.
next: How do I protect my shoulder?

How do I avoid injuries?

topics.covers: The visitor's knees hurt during or after tennis, or they ask about knee pain from playing.
topics.answer: If your knee hurts, stop playing and rest it. Tennis puts a lot of stopping, starting and twisting through the knees, and worn shoes, hard courts and weak hip and thigh muscles can all add to the load. If the pain is sharp, the knee swells, locks or gives way, or the pain lasts more than a few days, see a doctor or physical therapist.

topics.covers: The visitor's lower back hurts during or after tennis, or they ask about back pain from serving or twisting.
topics.answer: If your back hurts, stop playing and rest it rather than pushing through. Tennis loads the lower back through rotation and the arch of the serve, so bending your knees, using your legs and building core strength all help protect it. If the pain is sharp, spreads down a leg, comes with numbness or tingling, or lasts more than a few days, see a doctor or physical therapist.

How do I avoid injuries?

topics.covers: The visitor rolled, twisted or sprained their ankle on court, or their ankle hurts from playing.
topics.answer: If you roll your ankle, stop playing straight away and don't try to finish the set. Rest it and keep it raised. If you can't put weight on it, it swells or bruises a lot, the pain is sharp, or it still hurts after a few days, see a doctor or physical therapist. Once it has healed, balance exercises and proper tennis shoes help keep it from happening again.

topics.covers: The visitor has calf pain or a tight calf, or pain at the back of the ankle or heel (the Achilles area), while playing.
topics.answer: If your calf or the back of your ankle hurts, stop playing. A sudden, sharp pain there, especially one that feels like being kicked or hit, needs a doctor's check soon, so don't try to walk it off. For milder pain that lasts more than a few days, see a doctor or physical therapist. Warming up well and stretching your calves after play help keep them healthy.

topics.covers: The visitor gets blisters on their hands or feet from tennis, or asks how to prevent or treat them.
topics.answer: Blisters come from rubbing, so the fix is cutting down friction. On the hand, keep the grip fresh and dry with a new overgrip; on the feet, wear well-fitting tennis shoes and moisture-wicking socks, and break new shoes in slowly. If you feel a hot spot, stop and cover it with tape or a blister bandage before it opens. Keep blisters clean, and see a doctor if one looks infected, or the pain is sharp or lasts.

topics.covers: The visitor asks in general how to avoid or prevent tennis injuries.
topics.answer: You can lower your injury risk with a few habits: warm up before you play, increase how much you play gradually, wear proper tennis shoes, and do some strength work for your legs, core and shoulders. Good technique matters too, because it spreads the load through your whole body instead of your arm. And stop when something hurts, then see a doctor or physical therapist if the pain is sharp or lasts.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to play tennis safely as a senior or older adult, or how to adjust warm-up, recovery and play for age. Whether they are too old to start learning is improve_adult_start.
topics.answer: To keep playing safely as you get older, give yourself a longer warm-up, allow more recovery between sessions, and consider doubles, which needs less running. Tennis is a sport you can play for life, and many people keep playing well into older age. If you have heart, joint or other health conditions, check with your doctor first. Stop if something hurts, and see a doctor or physical therapist if the pain is sharp or lasts.

topics.covers: The visitor is coming back to tennis after an injury or surgery and asks how to return safely. Coming back after a long break without an injury is improve_comeback.
topics.answer: After an injury, get the all-clear from your doctor or physical therapist before you play, then ease back in over a few weeks. Start with short sessions of easy rallying, add serves and match play gradually, and leave a rest day between sessions at first. Stop and get it checked if the old pain comes back, or if any new pain is sharp or lasts.

topics.covers: The visitor is out of shape, overweight or unfit and asks whether they can still start playing tennis or need to get fit first.
topics.answer: Yes, you can start tennis without getting fit first: playing is one of the nicest ways to get fitter. Begin with short sessions, rest whenever you need to, and start with gentle rallies close to the net and doubles, which ask for less running. If you have a health condition or haven't exercised in a long time, check with your doctor before you begin.

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether tennis is good exercise or what the health benefits of playing tennis are.
topics.answer: Yes, tennis is very good exercise. It works your heart and lungs through repeated bursts of running, builds leg strength, balance and coordination, and keeps your reactions sharp. It's also social, which helps people keep playing for years, and you can adjust the effort by choosing singles or doubles.

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether to wear a brace, support, strap or tape on a sore wrist, knee, ankle or elbow when playing.
topics.answer: A brace or tape can make a sore joint feel more supported, but it doesn't fix the cause, and playing through pain can make things worse. If something hurts, stop and rest it first. If the pain is sharp or lasts, see a doctor or physical therapist, who can tell you whether a brace would help and which kind to use.

topics.covers: The visitor asks about sunscreen, sunburn or protecting their skin from the sun during outdoor tennis.
topics.answer: Wear a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher on all exposed skin, applied about 15 minutes before you play. Reapply at least every two hours, and sooner if you sweat a lot. A hat, sunglasses, and playing in the early morning or evening also cut your sun exposure, especially in summer.

topics.answer: Stop playing immediately and get medical help: chest pain or pressure, fainting, severe breathlessness or a racing, irregular heartbeat during exercise can be serious. If the symptoms are happening now or are severe, call emergency services right away. Even if they pass, see a doctor before you play again.

topics.covers: The visitor asks what the Eastern forehand grip is or how to find it, the shake-hands grip. About holding the racket, not a forehand that misses (tip_forehand_net, tip_forehand_long) or choosing between grips (ground_which_grip).
topics.answer: The Eastern forehand grip is the shake-hands grip. Lay your palm flat on the strings, slide it down to the handle and wrap your fingers around, so your palm sits behind the handle on the same side as the hitting face. It's easy to learn, good for flatter shots and handles low balls well, which makes it a fine first grip.
next: What is a semi-Western grip?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what a semi-Western grip is, how to hold it, or why so many players use it for topspin forehands. Defines this one grip; choosing between grips is ground_which_grip.
topics.answer: To hold a semi-Western grip, start from the Eastern shake-hands grip and turn your hand a little further under the handle, so your palm faces more upward behind it. That makes it easy to swing low to high, which gives you topspin and helps with high-bouncing balls. It's the most common forehand grip today. The trade-off is that very low balls are a little harder to dig out.
next: What is a Western grip?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what a full Western forehand grip is, or about its pros and cons for heavy topspin. Defines this one grip, not the Eastern or semi-Western.
topics.answer: A Western grip puts your palm almost underneath the handle, further round than semi-Western. It makes heavy topspin and high balls feel natural, but low balls and flat, fast shots get harder, and it takes more effort to hit through the court. Some strong players use it, but most people are better off with an Eastern or semi-Western grip.
next: What is a semi-Western grip?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what the Continental (hammer) grip is, how to find it, or which shots use it in general. About the grip itself; which grip to serve with is serve_grip and which grip to volley with is serve_volley_grip.
topics.answer: The Continental grip is the hammer grip: hold the racket with the edge of the frame pointing at the ground, as if you were about to hammer a nail with it. It's the grip for serves, volleys, overheads, slices and drop shots, because the racket face can open or close naturally. It's awkward for topspin forehands, so most players switch to an Eastern or semi-Western for those.

topics.covers: The visitor asks which forehand grip they should use or which is best for a beginner, comparing Eastern, semi-Western and Western in general. A recommendation, not a definition of one grip.
topics.answer: For most players, an Eastern or semi-Western forehand grip is the best place to start. Eastern is easier for flatter shots and low balls, semi-Western makes topspin and high balls easier, and both work at any level. I'd avoid a full Western grip at first. Whichever you choose, stick with it long enough to get used to it before you judge it.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to change grips quickly between forehand and backhand, or between groundstrokes and volleys, during a rally.
topics.answer: Let your other hand do the work. Keep it lightly on the throat of the racket in the ready position, and as you turn for the shot, use it to spin the handle into the new grip while your hitting hand stays loose. After every shot, come back to your ready grip. Practise it slowly while shadowing swings until it happens without thinking.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how tightly to hold the racket, whether their grip is too tight, or about a tense arm while hitting. Grip pressure only, not a general wish for more power (tip_power) or elbow pain (tip_tennis_elbow).
topics.answer: Hold the racket firmly enough that it won't twist, but not tightly: about a 3 or 4 on a scale of 1 to 10. A loose hand lets the racket head speed up through the ball, and it firms up on its own at contact. If your forearm tires quickly or your knuckles go white, you're squeezing too hard. Try relaxing your fingers between every point.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to hit a forehand, the basic steps of the forehand, or for beginner forehand technique. A step-by-step how-to, not a forehand going into the net or long (tip_forehand_net, tip_forehand_long).
topics.answer: A basic forehand has four steps. Turn your shoulders sideways as soon as you see the ball coming to your forehand, with the racket back and your other hand pointing at the ball. Let the racket drop below the ball, then swing low to high and meet it out in front of your front hip. Finish over your opposite shoulder, then recover to the ready position.

Where should I make contact?
What should my follow-through look like?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to hit a two-handed backhand or where each hand goes on the handle. A how-to for learning the stroke, not a weak or avoided backhand (tip_backhand) or choosing one or two hands (ground_one_or_two).
topics.answer: For a right-hander, the right hand holds a Continental grip at the bottom of the handle and the left hand sits just above it in a left-handed forehand grip. Turn your shoulders early, take the racket back with both hands, then swing low to high and meet the ball in front of your front hip. Think of it as a left-handed forehand, with the left arm doing most of the work, and finish over your right shoulder.
next: Should I use a one or two-handed backhand?

How do I switch grips quickly?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to hit a one-handed backhand: the grip, the turn and the swing. A how-to for learning the stroke, not a weak or avoided backhand (tip_backhand).
topics.answer: Use an Eastern backhand grip, with the knuckle of your index finger on top of the handle, so the racket face stays firm at contact. Turn your shoulders well, with your other hand holding the throat of the racket on the way back. Step in and meet the ball further in front than you would with two hands, then let your arms separate as you swing up, with the hitting arm extended.
next: Should I use a one or two-handed backhand?
How do I hit a slice backhand?
How do I handle high balls?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether to use a one-handed or two-handed backhand, which is better, or whether to switch from one to the other. A choice between the two, not how to hit either.
topics.answer: Either can be excellent, but the two-handed backhand is easier for most people to learn. The second hand adds stability on fast and high balls, which makes it a good default for kids and beginners. A one-hander gives more reach and pairs naturally with a slice, but it needs more strength and better timing. If yours already works, there's no need to switch.
next: How do I hit a two-handed backhand?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what topspin is or how to hit it, or wants more spin on their groundstrokes. A how-to on spin, not specifically a forehand flying long (tip_forehand_long).
topics.answer: Topspin makes the ball rotate forward, so it dips down into the court and bounces up higher. To hit it, drop the racket head below the ball, keep the face roughly straight up and down, and swing from low to high, brushing up the back of the ball. A relaxed wrist and a finish over your shoulder help. Start slowly with a partner and let the spin, not the speed, do the work.
next: What is a semi-Western grip?

What should my follow-through look like?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to hit a slice or underspin groundstroke, usually the backhand slice, or when to use slice from the baseline. Not a slice serve (serve_slice) or a drop shot (ground_drop_shot).
topics.answer: Slice is backspin: the ball floats, then stays low and skids after the bounce. Use a Continental grip, start the racket a little above the ball with the face slightly open, and swing forward and down through the ball, not just down. Keep the follow-through long toward the target. It's great for defense, for low balls and for changing the pace, but aim deep so it doesn't sit up.
next: What is the Continental grip?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what a flat groundstroke is, how it differs from topspin, or when to hit flatter. Groundstrokes only, not the flat serve (serve_flat).
topics.answer: A flat shot has little spin, so it travels fast and low but has less margin over the net. Hit it with a more level swing straight through the ball. It works best on a high, short ball close to the net, when you want to finish the point. For most rally balls, some topspin is safer, because it pulls the ball down into the court.
next: How do I hit topspin?

topics.covers: The visitor asks where to make contact with the ball: how far in front, how far from the body, or how high. Position relative to the body, not when in the bounce to hit (ground_bounce_timing).
topics.answer: Meet the ball in front of your body, about level with your front hip and roughly at waist height, with enough room that your arm isn't cramped. A one-handed backhand is met a little further in front, and a two-hander slightly closer. If the ball keeps getting beside or behind you, start your preparation earlier rather than swinging faster.
next: When should I hit the ball after the bounce?
