topics.covers: The visitor asks when to hit the ball after it bounces: on the rise, at the top of the bounce, or as it drops. Timing in the bounce, not where the ball is next to the body (ground_contact_point).
topics.answer: For most rally shots, hit the ball at the top of its bounce or just as it starts to drop, ideally between your waist and chest. Taking it on the rise, before it peaks, gives your opponent less time, but it's harder to time. Letting it drop low is easier but pushes you further back. Move your feet so the ball arrives at a height you like.
next: How do I handle high balls?
How do I handle low balls?
Where should I make contact?

topics.covers: The visitor asks where the follow-through should finish on a forehand or backhand, or what a windshield-wiper finish is.
topics.answer: Let the racket keep going after contact: a full follow-through keeps the swing smooth and adds control. On a forehand, finish up over your opposite shoulder, or across your body at chest height with the racket face turned over for more topspin, which some call a windshield-wiper finish. On a two-hander, finish over your hitting-side shoulder. Stopping the racket at contact usually means you're steering the ball.
next: How do I hit topspin?
How do I hit a forehand?
Where should I make contact?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to prepare earlier, what a unit turn is, or how big the backswing should be. Preparation of the upper body and racket, not being late because of footwork (tip_footwork).
topics.answer: Start your preparation with a unit turn: as soon as you know which side the ball is coming to, turn your shoulders and hips together so the racket goes back with your body. That one move does most of the backswing for you, so the arm doesn't need a big loop. A shorter, earlier backswing is more reliable than a big, late one, especially against fast balls.
next: Where should I make contact?
Should I hit open or closed stance?
What is a split step?

topics.covers: The visitor asks about open, closed or neutral stance on groundstrokes, which to use, or whether to step forward into the ball.
topics.answer: Use a neutral stance when you have time and an open stance when you're rushed or pulled wide. In a neutral stance you step forward with your front foot, which is the easiest to learn and good for balls you can move into. In an open stance your feet stay more side by side, facing the net, and you load on your outside leg, which is quicker on wide and fast balls, especially on the forehand. Learn neutral first.
next: How do I get to wide balls?
How do I prepare earlier?
How do I hit a forehand?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what to do with the non-hitting arm or free hand on a forehand, or why coaches say to point at the ball.
topics.answer: On a forehand, your non-hitting arm helps you turn and stay balanced. Reach it out across your body toward the ball as you prepare, which turns your shoulders, then pull it in toward your chest as you swing, which helps your body rotate. Letting it hang by your side usually means you've turned less, so your arm ends up doing all the work.
next: How do I hit a forehand?
How do I prepare earlier?
How do I hit topspin?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to hit a lob or when to lob, either a high defensive lob or an attacking lob over a net player. Hitting a lob, not dealing with being lobbed (serve_chase_lob).
topics.answer: Lob when your opponent is close to the net or when you're in trouble and need time. Open the racket face a little and lift the ball from low to high, aiming well over their reach and deep, near the baseline. A high defensive lob buys you time to recover, and a lower topspin lob over someone at the net can win the point. Short lobs get smashed, so err on the deep side.
next: How do I hit a passing shot?
How do I hit on the run?
How do I hit a drop shot?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to hit a drop shot off a bounce: the grip, the soft touch, or why their drop shots float or die in the net. Technique only; when to use one in a match is strategy_drop_shot_when, and a drop volley is serve_drop_volley.
topics.answer: To hit a drop shot, use a Continental grip and prepare as if for a normal shot, so it's hard to read. Then open the racket face and slice softly under the ball with relaxed hands, so it just clears the net and dies. If it floats deep, soften your hands and take more pace off; if it dies in the net, open the face a little more and lift it.
next: How do I hit a slice backhand?
How do I hit a lob?
What do I do with a short ball?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to hit a passing shot: keeping it low, dipping it at a net player's feet or going wide past them. The shot itself; a plan against someone who keeps rushing the net is strategy_net_rusher.
topics.answer: Against a net player, keep the ball low to make them volley up, or go wide past them. Topspin helps the ball dip at their feet. You don't need to win it in one shot: a low ball at their feet often sets up an easier pass or a lob on the next one. If they crowd the net, the lob is your other option.
next: How do I hit a lob?
How do I hit topspin?
How do I hit on the run?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to hit an approach shot, the groundstroke before moving to the net, and where to aim it. The shot itself, not when to come in (serve_when_net).
topics.answer: Hit an approach shot off a short ball, moving forward through it, and aim deep, often down the line, so the net is easier to cover. Hit with control rather than full power, then keep moving forward and split step as your opponent is about to hit. A deep slice or a solid topspin both work. The approach doesn't need to win the point; it needs to set up the volley.
next: When should I come to the net?
What do I do with a short ball?
Where should I stand at the net?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to hit a groundstroke on the run or when stretched wide, or which shot to play when pulled off the court.
topics.answer: When you're stretched wide, play for time, not a winner. Run with the racket already back, take a big last step, and hit a high, deep ball cross-court, a slice or a lob, which gives you the most room and time to recover. Going for a flat winner off balance rarely pays off. Once you've hit, push back toward the middle right away.
next: How do I get to wide balls?
Where should I go after hitting?
How do I hit a slice backhand?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what a split step is, how to do it, or exactly when to time it. An explanation of the move itself, not a complaint about being late or rushed (tip_footwork).
topics.answer: A split step is a small hop onto the balls of both feet, timed so you land just as your opponent hits the ball. Landing with your knees bent and feet a bit wider than your shoulders lets you push off in either direction straight away. Do it before every shot your opponent hits, on the baseline and at the net. Land too early or too late and you lose the spring.
next: What should my ready position look like?
Where should I go after hitting?
How do I get to wide balls?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to move back into position after hitting a shot: the footwork of recovering, side steps versus crossover steps, or how soon to start. Where to recover to is strategy_recover_position.
topics.answer: Recover with side steps when you only have a few steps to go and a crossover step when you have farther, so you stay balanced and facing the net. Start moving as soon as you finish your follow-through, rather than stopping to watch your shot. You don't always have to get all the way back: what matters is being balanced and ready to split step as your opponent hits.
next: What is a split step?
How do I get to wide balls?
How do I hit on the run?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what the ready position is, or how to stand while waiting for the ball: feet, knees, racket and grip.
topics.answer: Stand facing the net with your feet a bit wider than your shoulders, knees bent and weight on the balls of your feet. Hold the racket in front of you at about chest height, with your other hand lightly on the throat. Most players wait with their forehand grip on the baseline, or a Continental grip at the net. From here, split step as your opponent hits and turn as soon as you read the ball.
next: What is a split step?
How do I switch grips quickly?
How do I prepare earlier?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to get to wide balls, which first step to take, or how to cover the corners of the court faster. Moving sideways, not general lateness (tip_footwork).
topics.answer: Your first move to a wide ball is to turn and run, not shuffle. Pivot your outside foot toward the ball and take a crossover step with the other leg, turning your shoulders so the racket is back while you move. Use bigger steps to cover ground, then small ones to adjust, and often finish in an open stance so you can push back quickly.
next: How do I hit on the run?
Should I hit open or closed stance?
Where should I go after hitting?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to move forward to a short ball that lands mid-court and hit it, or why they miss easy short balls. Footwork and swing, not where to aim the attack (strategy_short_ball).
topics.answer: Move forward as soon as you see the ball is short, so you can take it at a good height instead of letting it drop. Use bigger steps to get there, then small ones to adjust. Because you're closer to the net, use a more compact swing and aim deep or to a corner, then keep moving in if it's a good approach. Many players miss short balls by overswinging.
next: How do I hit an approach shot?
When should I come to the net?
When should I hit flat?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to handle high-bouncing balls, heavy topspin kicking up to their shoulders, or high balls to the backhand.
topics.answer: You have two choices with a high ball: step back and let it drop to a comfortable height, or step in and take it earlier, before it climbs. Backing up is safer but gives ground, and stepping in takes time away from your opponent. On a high backhand, a slice is often the safest reply. A semi-Western forehand grip also makes high balls easier.
next: When should I hit the ball after the bounce?
How do I hit a slice backhand?
What is a semi-Western grip?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to hit low balls on groundstrokes, balls that skid or stay low, or how to bend for them. Groundstrokes, not low volleys at the net (serve_low_volley).
topics.answer: For low balls, bend your knees, not your back, so your eyes and racket get down near the ball. Keep the racket head below the ball and lift it with a low-to-high swing, or use a slice and stay low through the shot. Aim higher over the net than usual, since a low ball has to go up first. Staying down until after contact is the key.
next: How do I hit a slice backhand?
How do I hit topspin?
How do I handle high balls?

topics.covers: The visitor keeps hitting the ball off the frame, shanking or mishitting, or missing the sweet spot.
topics.answer: Mishits are usually about watching the ball and keeping your head still. Track the ball all the way into the strings and keep your head steady for a moment after contact, instead of looking up to see where it went. Shorten and slow your swing until you're hitting cleanly again, then build back up. A rushed, late swing also causes frame shots, so prepare early.
next: How do I prepare earlier?
Where should I make contact?
How tight should I hold the racket?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what an inside-out forehand is, or how and when to run around their backhand to hit a forehand.
topics.answer: An inside-out forehand is a forehand you hit from your backhand corner, after running around the ball, and send cross-court. Between two right-handers, that sends it to the other player's backhand. Hitting the same forehand down the line instead is called an inside-in forehand, and it makes a good surprise. It's a great weapon, but it leaves your forehand side open, so use it when the ball is slow or short enough to give you time.
next: How do I get to wide balls?
Where should I go after hitting?
How do I hit a forehand?

topics.covers: The visitor's groundstrokes land short in mid-court, they can't hit deep, or opponents keep attacking their short balls. About depth, not shots going into the net (tip_forehand_net) or long (tip_forehand_long).
topics.answer: Short balls usually come from too little height over the net or a swing that stops early. Aim higher, a racket length or more above the net, and swing through toward your target with a full follow-through, so the ball carries. Pick a target a few feet inside the baseline. A good practice game: rally with a partner and only count balls that land past the service line.
next: What should my follow-through look like?
How do I hit topspin?
Where should I make contact?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to aim or direct groundstrokes, the technique of hitting cross-court or down the line on purpose. How to aim, not which tactic to choose.
topics.answer: Direction comes mostly from where you meet the ball. Meet it a little further in front and the racket face points cross-court; meet it a little later, closer to your front hip, and it points down the line. Keep the same swing and let the contact point and racket face do the aiming. Practise by rallying cross-court only, then down the line only, with a partner.
next: Where should I make contact?
What is an inside-out forehand?
How do I hit an approach shot?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what grip to serve with, why coaches teach the Continental grip for serving, or whether a forehand or frying-pan grip is okay on the serve.
topics.answer: Serve with a Continental grip, the hammer grip, with the edge of the racket leading toward the ball. It lets your forearm turn through contact, which is where spin and easy speed come from. Many beginners serve with a forehand or frying-pan grip because it feels natural, but it only allows a flat push and limits you later. Switch early, even if the serve feels weaker at first.
next: What is the Continental grip?
How do I serve?
What is pronation?

topics.covers: The visitor asks where to stand to serve or how to place their feet: sideways stance, distance from the center mark in singles and doubles, or platform versus pinpoint stance.
topics.answer: Stand just behind the baseline, sideways to the net, with your front foot angled toward the net post. In singles, stand close to the center mark; in doubles, further toward the sideline. Some players keep their feet apart throughout, called a platform stance, while others bring the back foot up next to the front one, a pinpoint stance. Both work, so pick the one that feels balanced.
next: How do I toss the ball?
How do I serve?
How do I stop foot faulting?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to toss the ball for the serve or says their toss goes all over the place. The toss technique itself, not a serve landing in the net or long (tip_serve_net, tip_serve_long).
topics.answer: A steady toss comes from lifting the arm, not flicking the wrist. Hold the ball in your fingertips, keep your tossing arm straight and lift it from the shoulder, releasing the ball at about head height with your palm facing up. Toss it a little higher than you can reach with the racket, slightly in front and to your hitting side. Keep the arm up, pointing at the ball, after you let go.
next: What is the trophy position?
How do I hit a kick serve?
How do I serve?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what the trophy position in the serve is, or how their arms and body should look before swinging up.
topics.answer: The trophy position is the loaded moment just before you swing up. Your tossing arm points up at the ball, your hitting arm is bent with the elbow around shoulder height and the racket up behind your head, and your knees are bent, ready to push up. It's named after the pose on tennis trophies. Get there smoothly, with both arms rising together.
next: What is the racket drop?
How do I use my legs on the serve?
How do I toss the ball?

topics.covers: The visitor asks about the racket drop or back-scratch position in the serve, or why the racket should drop behind the back.
topics.answer: The racket drop is when the racket head falls down behind your back after the trophy position, just before you swing up at the ball. It happens naturally when your arm is relaxed and your legs push you up, and it gives the racket a long path to build speed. If you hold the racket stiff, it skips the drop and the serve loses pace. Think loose arm, not big arm.
next: What is pronation?
How do I use my legs on the serve?
What is the trophy position?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what pronation on the serve is, whether to snap their wrist, or how the forearm turns at contact.
topics.answer: Pronation is your forearm rotating inward through contact, so the racket face turns over and your palm ends up facing away from you, out to the side. It's how a Continental grip still meets the ball with a square face, and it adds easy speed. Don't force a wrist snap: with a relaxed arm and the right grip, it mostly happens on its own, and your thumb ends up pointing down after contact.
next: What grip should I serve with?
How do I hit a flat serve?
What is the racket drop?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to serve, the basic steps of the service motion, or how a beginner should learn to serve. A how-to, not a serve that misses (tip_serve_net, tip_serve_long, tip_double_fault).
topics.answer: A basic serve has five steps. Stand sideways with a Continental grip, then lift the toss and the racket together into the trophy position with your knees bent. Let the racket drop behind your back, then swing up and hit the ball at full stretch, slightly in front. Follow through across your body and land on your front foot. Start slowly, and add speed once it's smooth.
next: What grip should I serve with?
How do I toss the ball?
Which serve should I learn first?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to hit a flat serve, or a fast first serve with little spin. Not flat groundstrokes (ground_flat).
topics.answer: A flat serve is the fastest serve, with little spin. Toss slightly in front of you and into the court, hit straight through the back of the ball at full stretch, and let your forearm turn over through contact. With little spin it has the smallest margin, so most players use it as a first serve and aim for the middle of the box at first. Speed comes from the legs and a loose arm.
next: How do I hit a slice serve?
Where should I aim my serve?
How do I use my legs on the serve?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to hit a slice serve, or a serve that curves sideways. Not a slice groundstroke (ground_slice).
topics.answer: A slice serve curves sideways: for a right-hander, it bends to the left and stays fairly low. Use a Continental grip, toss slightly more to your hitting side, and brush across the outer side of the ball, as if hitting it at about three o'clock. It's reliable and can pull a returner wide. Give it more net clearance than a flat serve, and let the curve bring it into the box.
next: How do I hit a kick serve?
Where should I aim my serve?
Which serve should I learn first?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to hit a kick or topspin serve, a serve that bounces up high, or where to toss for it.
topics.answer: A kick serve has heavy topspin, so it clears the net high, dips into the box and jumps up after the bounce. Toss more above your head rather than out in front, bend your knees, and swing up and across the back of the ball, from about seven o'clock to one o'clock for a right-hander. It's the safest second serve once you have it, but expect it to take time to learn.
next: How do I hit a slice serve?
What is the racket drop?
Which serve should I learn first?

topics.covers: The visitor asks which serve to learn first, or the order to learn the flat, slice and kick serves.
topics.answer: Learn a basic, smooth serve with a Continental grip first; it naturally comes off the strings with a little slice. Once that's reliable, add a proper slice serve, then a kick serve, which needs the most technique. A faster flat serve comes along as your motion gets looser. One serve you trust matters more than three you don't.
next: How do I serve?
How do I hit a slice serve?
How do I hit a kick serve?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether an underhand serve is legal or allowed, or when to use one.
topics.answer: Yes, an underhand serve is legal. The rules only say you release the ball by hand and hit it before it touches the ground, standing behind the baseline, into the diagonal service box; nothing requires an overhead swing. Some players use it as a surprise against a returner standing far back. It's also a fine way to start points while a full serve is still coming together.
next: How do I serve?
Which serve should I learn first?
Where should I aim my serve?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to use their legs on the serve, bending the knees, or jumping up into the serve. Leg drive in the serve, not general power on groundstrokes (tip_power).
topics.answer: Your legs start the serve. Bend your knees as you reach the trophy position, then push up and slightly forward into the ball, so your body rises and the racket follows. Many players land inside the baseline on their front foot, which is fine because the ball is already gone. Don't force a jump: a good push up from the knees lifts you naturally.
next: How do I stop foot faulting?
What is the racket drop?
How do I hit a flat serve?

topics.covers: The visitor asks where to aim their serve, the targets in the service box (wide, body, the T), or how to make a serve harder to return. Aiming, not serves missing the box.
topics.answer: There are three main targets: wide toward the sideline, into the body, and down the T, where the center line meets the service line. Mixing them keeps the returner guessing, and serving to their weaker side, often the backhand, helps. Aim a little inside the lines for margin rather than at them. On second serves, the body or the backhand are the safest targets.
next: How do I hit a slice serve?
How do I hit a flat serve?
Do I need a serve routine?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to stop foot faulting in their technique, or whether jumping or landing inside the court during the serve is allowed. Fixing the feet, not a full explanation of the rule.
topics.answer: To stop foot faulting, start a few inches behind the baseline and keep your front foot still until you push up into the ball. The common foot fault is touching the baseline or the court inside it before you hit the ball, so jumping and landing inside afterward is fine. If your back foot slides up, let it stop beside your front foot, not past it. A toss too far in front can also drag your feet forward.
next: Where should I stand to serve?
How do I use my legs on the serve?
How do I toss the ball?

topics.covers: The visitor asks where to stand to return serve, how far back, or how far to the side. Return positioning, not missing returns against fast or spinning serves (tip_return).
topics.answer: Start near the baseline, roughly where you can reach a wide serve and a serve down the middle with a step or two. Against a big first serve, move back a little for more time; against a slow second serve, move in. Watch where the server stands and tosses, and adjust. Wherever you start, split step as they hit.
next: How do I attack a second serve?
What is a split step?
Where should I aim my serve?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to attack or take advantage of a weak or slow second serve when returning. Not handling fast first serves (tip_return).
topics.answer: Step in a little against a second serve, so you take the ball earlier and at a comfortable height. Use a fuller swing than on a first-serve return, but aim deep or to the server's weaker side rather than at the lines. You can also come forward behind a good return. Missing an attackable return is still an error, so keep your margin.
next: Where should I stand to return serve?
When should I come to the net?
How do I hit an approach shot?

topics.covers: The visitor asks which grip to use for volleys, or whether to change grips between forehand and backhand volleys. The volley grip only, not general net play or nerves (tip_volley).
topics.answer: Volley with a Continental grip, the hammer grip, on both sides. At the net there's rarely time to change grips, and the Continental lets you hit forehand and backhand volleys with a slightly open face, which adds a little underspin and control. It can feel weak on the backhand at first; using your other hand on the throat of the racket to take it back helps.
next: What is the Continental grip?
How do I hit a low volley?
Where should I aim my volleys?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to hit a low volley below net height, or says their low volleys go into the net. Specific to low balls at the net, not general volley technique (tip_volley).
topics.answer: For a low volley, bend your knees to bring your eyes and racket down to the ball, rather than dropping the racket head. Open the racket face a little and lift the ball over the net, aiming deep rather than trying to hit hard. A low volley is a setup shot: get it deep, move forward, and finish on the next, higher ball.
next: How do I hit a half volley?
Where should I aim my volleys?
What grip should I volley with?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what a half volley is, or how to hit a ball that bounces right at their feet while moving forward.
topics.answer: A half volley is a shot you hit just after the ball bounces, right at your feet, often while you're moving to the net. Get down low with your knees bent, use a very short backswing and keep the racket face steady, so you block the ball rather than swing at it. Aim deep and down the middle, then keep moving forward and split step for the next ball.
next: How do I hit a low volley?
Where should I stand at the net?
What is a split step?

topics.covers: The visitor asks for overhead or smash technique specifically: turning, footwork and contact on a lob. A how-to for the smash, not general net nerves or volleys (tip_volley).
topics.answer: As soon as you see the lob, turn sideways, bring the racket up behind your head early and point your other hand at the ball. Move back with side steps or crossover steps so the ball stays in front of you, then hit it at full stretch, like a serve. Place it rather than blasting it. Most missed smashes come from ending up under the ball because the feet stopped moving.
next: Should I let a lob bounce?
What if I get lobbed at the net?
How do I serve?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether to let a lob bounce before hitting an overhead, or when to smash it out of the air.
topics.answer: Let a very high lob bounce, especially in wind or sun, because it's easier to time after the bounce. Hit it out of the air when it's lower, when you're close to the net, or when waiting would push you back toward the baseline. When you let it bounce, stay sideways and give it plenty of room so it comes down in front of you.
next: How do I hit an overhead?
What if I get lobbed at the net?
Where should I stand at the net?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what to do when they get lobbed at the net and the ball goes over their head, how to chase down a lob, or why they keep getting lobbed.
topics.answer: If a lob goes over you, turn and run back rather than backpedaling, and run to the side of the ball so it lands in front of you. Once you get there, don't try anything fancy: hit a high, deep lob back to buy time to recover. If you keep getting lobbed, you may be standing too close to the net.
next: Where should I stand at the net?
How do I hit an overhead?
How do I hit a lob?

topics.covers: The visitor asks when to come to the net in singles, or whether they should rush the net. Choosing the moment, not how to hit the approach shot (ground_approach_shot).
topics.answer: Come in when you've hit a shot that puts your opponent in trouble: off a short ball you can approach on, or after pushing them wide or deep. Coming in behind a weak shot just gives them an easy pass. In doubles, players come to the net much more often. Choose your moments, then commit.
next: How do I hit an approach shot?
Where should I stand at the net?
How do I serve and volley?

topics.covers: The visitor asks where to stand at the net in singles, or how close to the net to get after coming in.
topics.answer: In singles, after an approach, aim to settle about halfway between the service line and the net, shading toward the side you hit to. Closer makes volleys easier but leaves you open to lobs; further back leaves you volleying from your feet. Keep moving forward after each volley if you can, and split step as your opponent hits.
next: What if I get lobbed at the net?
How do I hit a low volley?
Where should I aim my volleys?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to serve and volley, or what to do after serving to get to the net.
topics.answer: Serve and volley works best behind a serve that's well placed, not just fast. After the serve, move forward and split step around the service line as the returner hits. Make the first volley deep, often back toward the middle or to the open side, then close in for the next one. Low returns at your feet are the main danger, so stay down on them.
next: How do I hit a half volley?
Where should I aim my serve?
Where should I stand at the net?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to hit a drop volley, a soft volley out of the air that lands just over the net. Not a drop shot off the bounce (ground_drop_shot).
topics.answer: A drop volley takes the pace off the ball so it lands short. Loosen your grip at contact, open the racket face slightly and let the racket give a little, like catching the ball, rather than punching it. Use it when your opponent is deep behind the baseline, and aim for a corner. Against an opponent who's close in, a firm deep volley is safer.
next: Where should I aim my volleys?
How do I hit a drop shot?
How do I hit a low volley?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what a swinging volley is, or how to hit a high, floating ball out of the air from mid-court.
topics.answer: A swinging volley is a full groundstroke swing at a ball out of the air, usually a high, slow ball floating in mid-court. Use your normal forehand grip, swing low to high with topspin and keep your eyes on the ball, since there's no bounce to help your timing. Save it for slow, high balls; on anything fast or low, a regular volley is safer.
next: How do I hit an overhead?
When should I come to the net?
How do I hit topspin?

topics.covers: The visitor asks where to aim their volleys, or whether to volley deep or go for angles.
topics.answer: Hit low volleys deep, and save the angles for high balls when you're close to the net. A deep volley keeps your opponent back and gives you time to move in; a sharp angle wins points but is risky from further back. In singles, the open court is usually the target. In doubles, the feet of the net player or the gap between the two players are good targets.
next: How do I hit a low volley?
How do I hit a drop volley?
Where should I stand at the net?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how points are counted within a game: love, 15, 30, 40 and game, or how many points it takes to win a game.
topics.answer: A game goes to the first player to win four points, with a lead of at least two. The points are called love (zero), 15, 30 and 40, and the next point after 40 wins the game. If both players reach 40, it's deuce, and someone has to win two points in a row to take the game.
next: What happens at deuce?
How do you win a set?
Why is tennis scored 15, 30, 40?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what happens when the score reaches 40-40, how advantage works, or how to win a game from deuce.
topics.answer: At 40-40 the score is deuce, and you need two points in a row to win the game. Win the next point and you have the advantage; win the one after and the game is yours. If you lose the point after your advantage, the score goes back to deuce, and this can repeat as many times as it takes.
next: What is no-ad scoring?
What does deuce mean?
How do you win a set?

topics.covers: The visitor asks about no-ad scoring: playing a single deciding point at 40-40 instead of advantage, and who chooses the side for that point.
topics.answer: In no-ad scoring, a game at 40-40 is decided by one point instead of playing advantage, and whoever wins that point wins the game. The receiver chooses which side, deuce or ad, to receive from, and in doubles the receiving team chooses which player returns. Many leagues, college matches and casual groups use it to keep matches shorter, so check the format before you start.
next: What happens at deuce?
What is a match tiebreak?
What's a pro set?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to win a set, how many games are in a set, or whether a set can end 6-5 or 7-5.
topics.answer: A set goes to the first player to win six games with a lead of at least two. So 6-4 ends the set, but at 6-5 you play on: 7-5 wins it, and 6-6 usually means a tiebreak decides the set 7-6. A few formats play an advantage set instead, with no tiebreak, where play continues until someone leads by two games.
next: How does a tiebreak work?
How many sets are in a match?
What's a pro set?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how a tiebreak works at 6-6: how points are counted, the serving order in it, when to switch ends, and how many points win it.
topics.answer: A tiebreak is played at 6-6 and goes to the first player to reach seven points with a two-point lead, counted 1, 2, 3 instead of 15, 30, 40. The player due to serve serves the first point from the deuce side, then each player serves two points in turn, starting from the ad side. Players change ends after every six points, and the set is recorded as 7-6.
next: Who serves first after a tiebreak?
What is a match tiebreak?
What does 7-6(4) mean?

topics.covers: The visitor asks who serves first in the next set after a tiebreak, or whether players change ends after a set that ended in a tiebreak.
topics.answer: The player who received first in the tiebreak serves the first game of the next set. In other words, whoever served the opening point of the tiebreak receives to start the new set. The players also change ends after a tiebreak set, because the tiebreak counts as one game and the set totals 13 games, an odd number.
next: How does a tiebreak work?
When do you change ends?
How many sets are in a match?

topics.covers: The visitor asks about a match tiebreak or super tiebreak: the 10-point tiebreak played instead of a final set.
topics.answer: A match tiebreak, often called a super tiebreak, replaces a deciding third set when the match is tied at one set each. It's played like a normal tiebreak, but the winner is the first to reach 10 points with a two-point lead. It's common in doubles, junior events and many leagues, though formats vary, so confirm before the match.
next: How does a tiebreak work?
How many sets are in a match?
What is no-ad scoring?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how many sets are in a tennis match, best of three versus best of five, or how many sets you need to win.
topics.answer: Most matches are best of three sets, so the first to win two sets wins the match. Men's singles at the Grand Slams are best of five, where you need three sets. Leagues and casual matches often shorten things with a match tiebreak in place of a third set, or a single pro set, so the format depends on where you play.
next: What is a match tiebreak?
What's a pro set?
What are the Grand Slams?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what a pro set or eight-game set is, and how it is scored.
topics.answer: A pro set is a single set played to eight games instead of six, with a two-game lead needed to win. It's a shorter alternative to a full match, used in some leagues, practice matches and doubles events. At 8-8 a tiebreak usually decides it, but the exact format varies, so agree on it before you start.
next: How many sets are in a match?
How do you win a set?
What is no-ad scoring?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to decide who serves first, spinning a racket or tossing a coin, and what choices the winner of the toss has.
topics.answer: Before the warm-up, players toss a coin or spin a racket, and the winner chooses. They can pick to serve or receive first, and the opponent then picks the end. Or they can pick the end, and the opponent decides who serves. They can also hand the first choice to the opponent. In casual play, spinning a racket and calling up or down on the logo is the usual way.
next: Which side do you serve from first?
When do you change ends?
How do faults work?

topics.covers: The visitor asks which side to serve from, when to switch sides between points, or how players take turns serving games.
topics.answer: You serve the first point of every game from the right of the center mark, then alternate sides each point: left, right, left. The serve goes diagonally to the box across the net. One player serves a whole game, then the opponent serves the next, alternating like that for the rest of the match.
next: Where does the serve have to land?
What is a foot fault?
What happens if I serve from the wrong side?

topics.covers: The visitor asks where a serve has to land, which service box counts, whether a serve on the line is good, or whether a serve in the doubles alley is in.
topics.answer: A serve must land in the service box diagonally opposite you, before the receiver hits it. The lines around that box count as in, so a serve that touches the service line, center line or sideline of the box is good. The service box is the same in singles and doubles, so a serve landing in the doubles alley is a fault.
next: How do faults work?
What is a let serve?
What is the service box?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what counts as a fault, how many serves you get, or what a double fault is and what it costs.
topics.answer: You get two serves to start each point. A serve is a fault if it doesn't land in the correct box, including one that hits the net and drops back, or if you swing and miss the ball entirely. Foot faults count too. After one fault you take a second serve, and if that one is also a fault, it's a double fault and you lose the point.
next: What is a foot fault?
What is a let serve?
Can I catch my toss and toss again?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what a foot fault is, where the server must stand, or whether their feet can touch or cross the baseline when serving.
topics.answer: A foot fault is when the server touches the baseline or the court inside it with either foot before hitting the ball. You must also stand behind the baseline between the center mark and the sideline, and you can't walk or run into the serve. Your feet can leave the ground and land inside the court after you hit the ball, which is how most players serve.
next: How do faults work?
Which side do you serve from first?
Where can players stand?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what happens when a serve clips the net and lands in, what a let serve is, or how many lets are allowed.
topics.answer: If a serve touches the net and still lands in the correct box, it's a let and you replay that serve. It doesn't erase an earlier fault, so a let on your second serve gives you one more second serve. There's no limit on lets. If the serve clips the net and lands out, it's a normal fault. A few formats play serves off the net as live, so check if you're unsure.
next: How do faults work?
When else is a point replayed?
Where does the serve have to land?

topics.covers: The visitor asks when a point is replayed because of an outside interruption, such as a ball rolling onto the court from another court in the middle of a point.
topics.answer: A point is replayed as a let when something outside the players' control interrupts it, such as a ball rolling onto your court from the next one. Call let straight away, before the point plays out, and replay the whole point. A serve is also replayed if the receiver wasn't ready, as long as they didn't try to return it.
next: What is a let serve?
What if the ball hits me?
What counts as a hindrance?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether a ball that touches the line is in or out during a rally.
topics.answer: A ball that touches any part of the line is in. The lines belong to the court they surround, so even a tiny part of the ball touching the outside edge of the line counts as good. Only a ball that lands completely beyond the line, with clear space between the ball and the line, is out.
next: Where does the serve have to land?
What if the ball hits the net post?
What lines are in for doubles?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how many times the ball can bounce, whether you can hit it before it bounces, or whether the receiver can volley a serve.
topics.answer: You must hit the ball before it bounces twice on your side, so one bounce is the limit. You're also allowed to hit it before it bounces at all, which is a volley. The one exception is the serve: the receiver has to let it bounce in the box first, and volleying a serve loses the point.
next: Can I hit the ball twice?
What if the ball hits me?
What's a volley?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether hitting the ball twice in one swing (a double hit or carry) is legal, whether you can switch hands or use two hands, or whether throwing the racket at the ball counts.
topics.answer: An accidental double hit during one continuous swing is legal, but deliberately hitting the ball twice or carrying it on the strings loses the point. You can hold the racket in either hand, switch hands during a point, or use two hands. The ball does have to be hit with the racket in your hand: a thrown racket that hits the ball loses the point.
next: What if the ball hits me?
Can I touch the net?
How many bounces are allowed?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether you can touch the net, net post or opponent's side of the court during a point, with your body, racket or clothing.
topics.answer: If you, your racket or anything you're wearing touches the net, the net posts or your opponent's side of the court while the ball is in play, you lose the point. That includes running into the net after hitting a winner, if the ball hasn't bounced twice yet. Once the point is over, touching the net doesn't matter.
next: Can I reach over the net?
What if the ball hits me?
Can I hit the ball twice?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether you can reach over the net to hit the ball, or follow through over the net after hitting.
topics.answer: You have to let the ball cross to your side before you hit it, but your racket may follow through over the net afterward, as long as you don't touch the net. There's one exception: if the ball bounces on your side and spin or wind carries it back over the net, you may reach across to play it.
next: Can I touch the net?
What if the ball hits the net post?
How many bounces are allowed?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what happens if the ball hits a player before bouncing, or if a player catches a ball that was going out.
topics.answer: If the ball hits you, or anything you're wearing or carrying other than your racket, before it bounces, you lose the point. That's true even if you're standing well outside the court, so catching a ball that was clearly going out still costs you the point. On a serve, a ball that hits the receiver before bouncing is the server's point.
next: What if the ball hits the fence?
Can I touch the net?
Can I hit the ball twice?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether a rally shot that clips the net cord, hits the net post, or goes around the outside of the net post and lands in is good.
topics.answer: In a rally, a ball that clips the top of the net and lands in is good, and play continues. A shot that hits the net post and lands in is also good, and so is a ball that goes around the outside of the post, even below net height, as long as it lands in. On a serve, though, a ball that hits the net post is a fault.
next: What if the ball hits the fence?
What is a let serve?
Is a ball on the line in?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what happens when the ball hits the fence, lights, ceiling, a bench or another fixture, before or after bouncing.
topics.answer: If your shot hits the fence, a light, the ceiling or anything else outside the court before it bounces, you lose the point. If it bounces in the court first and then hits the fence, it was a good shot, and your opponent loses the point for not getting it back. Some indoor clubs have local rules for low ceilings, so ask when you play somewhere new.
next: What if the ball hits me?
What if the ball hits the net post?
Is a ball on the line in?

topics.covers: The visitor asks when players switch ends or change sides of the court, and how long rest breaks are at changeovers and between sets.
topics.answer: Players change ends after the first game of each set, then after every two games, so after the first, third, fifth and every other odd-numbered game. In a tiebreak you change after every six points. Under ITF rules you get up to 90 seconds at changeovers, no rest after the first game of a set, and two minutes between sets.
next: How does a tiebreak work?
Who serves first after a tiebreak?
How do you decide who serves first?

topics.covers: The visitor asks about the serving and receiving order in doubles: which partner serves, how the order rotates, and which side each partner receives on.
topics.answer: In doubles, each team decides who serves its first game, and partners alternate their team's service games, so all four players serve in a fixed rotation. For receiving, each team picks one partner for the deuce side and one for the ad side, and they stay there for the whole set. Both the serving order and the receiving sides can change at the start of each new set.
next: What lines are in for doubles?
Can both partners hit the ball?
What happens if I serve from the wrong side?

topics.covers: The visitor asks which court lines count in singles versus doubles, or whether the doubles alleys are in during a rally.
topics.answer: Singles uses the inner sidelines, and doubles uses the outer sidelines, which add the alleys on each side. The baseline is the same for both. In doubles the alleys are in for every shot after the serve, but the serve itself must still land in the normal service box, so a serve in the alley is a fault.
next: What is the doubles alley?
Can both partners hit the ball?
Where does the serve have to land?

topics.covers: The visitor asks doubles rules about who may hit the ball, both partners hitting it, rackets clashing, or a serve that hits the server's partner.
topics.answer: After the serve is returned, either partner can hit any ball, no matter where they stand, but only one of you may touch it. The serve itself must be returned by the receiver, so if the receiver's partner touches it, the serving team wins the point. If both partners' rackets hit the ball, your team loses the point, though a clash of rackets is fine if only one touched it. A serve that hits the server's partner is a fault.
next: How does serving work in doubles?
What lines are in for doubles?
Where can players stand?

topics.covers: The visitor asks where players are legally allowed to stand under the rules, such as whether the receiver or a doubles partner can stand anywhere (not tactical positioning).
topics.answer: The receiver can stand anywhere on their own side, inside or outside the court, even close to the net. In doubles, both the server's partner and the receiver's partner can also stand anywhere on their side. Only the server has a fixed place: behind the baseline, between the center mark and the sideline. Nobody may touch the other side of the court during a point.
next: What is a foot fault?
Can both partners hit the ball?
Is the receiver allowed to volley the serve?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what happens if someone serves from the wrong side, serves out of turn, or the wrong partner serves in doubles.
topics.answer: Fix it as soon as you notice, and the points already played still count. If you served from the wrong side, switch to the correct side for the next point. If the wrong player served, the right one takes over straight away, but if a whole game finished before anyone noticed, keep the new order from then on.
next: Which side do you serve from first?
How does serving work in doubles?
What if we disagree on the score?

topics.covers: The visitor asks about hindrance: an opponent shouting or distracting them during a point, a spare ball or hat falling during play, or talking during points.
topics.answer: If an opponent deliberately hinders you, for example by shouting as you hit, you win the point. If it's accidental, such as a spare ball or a hat falling onto the court, the other side can call a let and the point is replayed, but if it keeps happening it can count as hindrance and cost the point. Doubles partners can talk while the ball is coming toward them, but should stay quiet while it's heading to the opponents.
next: When else is a point replayed?
What if we disagree on the score?
Do official rules apply in casual games?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether the server can catch a bad toss and toss again, or what happens if they swing at the toss and miss.
topics.answer: Yes, if your toss is off, you can catch it or let it drop and toss again with no penalty, as long as you don't swing at it. If you swing and miss, that counts as a fault. Re-tossing now and then is normal, but doing it over and over can bother your opponent, so work on a steadier toss.
next: How do faults work?
What is a foot fault?
Does the receiver have to be ready?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether the server must wait for the receiver to be ready, about quick serving, or how long the receiver can take.
topics.answer: The server must wait until the receiver is ready, and a serve hit before then is replayed. The receiver, in turn, has to play at the server's reasonable pace and can't stall. If the receiver tries to return the serve, they're treated as ready, so they can't claim afterward that they weren't.
next: When else is a point replayed?
Can I catch my toss and toss again?
When do you change ends?

topics.covers: The visitor asks the rule for who announces the score and which player's score is said first, what a call like 15-30 means for the server, or how to settle a disputed or forgotten score.
topics.answer: In casual play the server announces the score: the game score before the first point of each game, and the point score before every point, with the server's score first. So 15-30 means the server has 15. If you disagree, count the points you both agree on and replay only the disputed ones, or go back to the last score you both accept.
next: How are points counted in a game?
Do official rules apply in casual games?
What does 7-6(4) mean?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether official rules apply in casual or friendly games, or what format to agree on before a social match with no umpire.
topics.answer: Yes, the official rules still apply, but in casual play you agree on the format before you start, since there's no umpire to set it. Settle how many sets, whether a tiebreak is played at 6-6, whether you'll use no-ad scoring and how long the warm-up lasts. Each player calls the lines on their own side, and the server keeps the score aloud.
next: What is no-ad scoring?
Who calls out the score?
What's a pro set?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what the word love means in tennis, why zero is called love, or what a love game is.
topics.answer: Love means zero in tennis, so 15-love is 15-0 and a love game is a game won without the opponent winning a point. Nobody knows for sure where the word comes from. One popular theory links it to the French l'oeuf, meaning egg, for the shape of a zero, and another says it comes from playing for love, with nothing at stake.
next: Why is tennis scored 15, 30, 40?
What does deuce mean?
What is a bagel?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what the word deuce means or where it comes from, or what score calls like ad in, ad out, 15-all and 30-all mean.
topics.answer: Deuce is the call for a tied score of 40-40, or any tie after that within the game. The word is generally thought to come from the French for two, since a player then needs two points in a row. Ad in means the server has the advantage, ad out means the receiver has it, and all means tied, as in 15-all or 30-all.
next: What happens at deuce?
What does love mean?
Why is tennis scored 15, 30, 40?

topics.covers: The visitor asks why tennis is scored 15, 30, 40 instead of 1, 2, 3, or where the scoring system came from.
topics.answer: Nobody knows for certain why tennis counts 15, 30, 40. The most common theory is that scores were once kept on a clock face, moving a quarter of the way round each point: 15, 30, 45, then game at 60. The 45 is said to have been shortened to 40, but historians haven't settled it, so treat any single story as a guess.
next: What does love mean?
How are points counted in a game?
Where did tennis come from?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what an ace is, or the difference between an ace and a service winner.
topics.answer: An ace is a legal serve that the receiver doesn't touch at all, so the server wins the point outright. A service winner is a serve the receiver gets a racket on but can't return into play. Both win the point straight from the serve, but only the untouched one counts as an ace in match statistics.
next: What is a winner?
What is an unforced error?
What is a break point?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what the term winner means for a shot, as in hitting a winner or a clean winner.
topics.answer: A winner is a shot that lands in and that your opponent can't touch, so it wins the point outright. If they get a racket on it but can't return it, it's usually counted as a forced error instead. In match statistics, winners are often set against unforced errors to show how well someone played.
next: What is an unforced error?
What is an ace?
What is a rally?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what the terms unforced error and forced error mean, or the difference between them.
topics.answer: An unforced error is a miss on a ball you had the time and position to play well, like netting an easy rally ball. A forced error is a miss caused by your opponent's good shot, such as a fast ball stretched out of reach. The line between them is a judgment call, so different statisticians can count the same match differently.
next: What is a winner?
What is a rally?
What is a break point?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what the word rally means in tennis, what rally length is, or the difference between rallying and playing points.
topics.answer: A rally is the exchange of shots back and forth during a point, starting with the return of serve. Rally length is how many shots it lasts. Players also use rallying to mean hitting back and forth without keeping score, as in a warm-up or a practice session.
next: What is a winner?
What is an unforced error?
What is a groundstroke?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what a bagel, double bagel or breadstick is, or what winning in straight sets means.
topics.answer: A bagel is a set won 6-0, named for the round shape of the zero, and a double bagel is a match won 6-0, 6-0. A breadstick is a set won 6-1, because the 1 looks like a breadstick. Winning in straight sets means winning the match without losing a set.
next: What does love mean?
What does 7-6(4) mean?
What is a break point?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what holding serve, breaking serve or breaking back means, or what it means for a set to be on serve.
topics.answer: Holding serve means winning a game you serve. Breaking serve means winning a game your opponent serves, which matters because the server usually has the edge. Breaking back means winning a game on your opponent's serve after they broke yours, which levels the set again, and a set is on serve when neither player is ahead by a break.
next: What is a break point?
What is an ace?
What does deuce mean?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what the terms break point, set point, match point or championship point mean.
topics.answer: A break point is a point where the receiver can win the server's game with one more point, such as 30-40. A set point is one point from winning the set, and a match point is one point from winning the match. A championship point is a match point in the final of a tournament.
next: What does breaking serve mean?
What is a bagel?
What does deuce mean?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to read a written tennis score like 6-4 3-6 6-3 or 7-6(4), including the number in brackets after a tiebreak.
topics.answer: Each pair of numbers is one set, written as games won, usually from the winner's side, so 6-4, 3-6, 6-3 means the winner took the first and third sets. In 7-6(4), the number in brackets is the loser's points in the tiebreak, so it ended 7-4. A final pair like 10-8 usually means a match tiebreak decided it.
next: How does a tiebreak work?
What is a match tiebreak?
What is a bagel?

topics.covers: The visitor asks the names of the lines on a tennis court: baseline, service line, center service line, center mark and sidelines.
topics.answer: The baseline is the back line at each end, and the center mark is the short notch in its middle. The service line runs across the court parallel to the net, marking the back of the service boxes, and the center service line splits those boxes in two. The sidelines run the length of the court, with the inner pair for singles and the outer pair for doubles.
next: What is the service box?
What is the doubles alley?
How big is a tennis court?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what the service box is, or what the deuce side and ad side (deuce court and ad court) are and why they are named that.
topics.answer: The service boxes are the two rectangles on each side of the net, between the net and the service line, and every serve must land in one of them. The deuce side is the right half from the player's view and the ad side is the left. The names come from scoring: at deuce you serve from the right, and advantage points are served from the left.
next: Where does the serve have to land?
What are the lines on a court called?
What is the doubles alley?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what the doubles alley or tramlines are.
topics.answer: The alley is the long strip down each side of the court between the singles and doubles sidelines, about four and a half feet wide. In British English it's called the tramlines. It's out in singles and in during doubles rallies, though never for the serve.
next: What lines are in for doubles?
How big is a tennis court?
What are the lines on a court called?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how big a tennis court is, its length and width, or how high the net is.
topics.answer: A tennis court is 78 feet long. It's 27 feet wide for singles and 36 feet wide for doubles. The service line sits 21 feet from the net, and the net is 3 feet high at the center and 3 feet 6 inches at the posts. Young players using slower balls often play on smaller courts.
next: What are the lines on a court called?
What is the doubles alley?
What is no man's land?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what no man's land means on a tennis court.
topics.answer: No man's land is the area between the service line and the baseline. It gets the name because balls often land at your feet there, which makes them awkward to hit, so players try not to linger in it. You pass through it when moving forward to the net rather than stopping in the middle.
next: What are the lines on a court called?
What is a groundstroke?
How big is a tennis court?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what basic stroke names mean: groundstroke, forehand, backhand, volley and half volley (definitions, not how to hit them).
topics.answer: A groundstroke is any shot hit after the ball bounces, usually from near the baseline. A forehand is hit on your racket-hand side and a backhand on the other side. A volley is hit before the ball bounces, usually near the net, and a half volley is hit just after the bounce, with the ball still very low.
next: What do lob and drop shot mean?
What is a rally?
What is no man's land?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what shot names mean: lob, drop shot, overhead or smash, passing shot and approach shot (definitions, not how to hit them).
topics.answer: A lob is a high shot over an opponent at the net, and a drop shot is a soft one that lands just over the net. An overhead, or smash, is hit above your head like a serve, usually against a lob. A passing shot goes past an opponent at the net, and an approach shot is the one you hit as you move forward to the net.
next: What is a groundstroke?
What do moonball and tweener mean?
What is a winner?

topics.covers: The visitor asks about tennis slang: moonball, tweener, net cord and similar casual terms.
topics.answer: A moonball is a very high, loopy rally shot that bounces up high. A tweener is a shot hit between your legs, usually while running back to chase a lob. A net cord is a ball that clips the top of the net tape and drops over, which is good in a rally.
next: What is a bagel?
What do lob and drop shot mean?
What if the ball hits the net post?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what singles, doubles and mixed doubles are, or the difference between singles and doubles.
topics.answer: Singles is one player against one, and doubles is two against two on the wider court that includes the alleys. Mixed doubles is doubles where each team has one man and one woman. Doubles puts more weight on net play and quick reactions, while singles asks more of your movement and fitness.
next: What is the doubles alley?
How does serving work in doubles?
What are the Grand Slams?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what the Grand Slams or majors are, when they are played, or what surface each is played on.
topics.answer: The four Grand Slams, or majors, are the biggest tournaments in tennis. The Australian Open is on hard courts in January, the French Open, or Roland Garros, is on clay from late May into June, Wimbledon is on grass from late June into July, and the US Open is on hard courts from late August into September.
next: What is a calendar Grand Slam?
What are the ATP and WTA?
Why does Wimbledon make players wear white?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what a calendar Grand Slam, a career Grand Slam or a Golden Slam means.
topics.answer: A calendar Grand Slam means winning all four majors in the same calendar year, which very few players have ever done. A career Grand Slam means winning each of the four at least once over a career. A Golden Slam adds an Olympic gold medal: strictly, all four majors and the gold in the same year, while collecting them all across a career is called a career Golden Slam.
next: What are the Grand Slams?
Is tennis in the Olympics?
How do tennis rankings work?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what the ATP and WTA are, how the professional tours are organized, or what Challenger and ITF events are.
topics.answer: The ATP runs the main professional tour for men and the WTA runs the one for women, with tournaments around the world for most of the year. Below them, men work their way up through ATP Challenger events and women through WTA 125 events, with the ITF World Tennis Tour as the entry level for both. The ITF, tennis's international federation, sets the rules of the game and runs the national team competitions.
next: How do tennis rankings work?
What are the Grand Slams?
What is the Davis Cup?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how professional ATP or WTA rankings work, how pros earn ranking points, or what defending points means.
topics.answer: Professional rankings are based on points earned at tournaments, with bigger events and deeper runs worth more. They generally work on a rolling 52 weeks, so points from an event drop off a year later, when that tournament comes around again. That's why players talk about defending points from the year before.
next: What are the ATP and WTA?
What are seeds and wildcards?
What are the Grand Slams?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what seeds, wildcards, qualifiers or lucky losers are in a tournament draw.
topics.answer: Seeds are the top-ranked entrants, placed apart in the draw so they can't meet in the early rounds. A wildcard is a spot the organizers give to a player who wouldn't otherwise get in. A qualifier won through a qualifying event before the main draw, and a lucky loser lost in qualifying but gets in when another player withdraws.
next: What is a walkover?
How do tennis rankings work?
What are the Grand Slams?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what a walkover, a retirement (ret), a bye or a default means in a tournament.
topics.answer: A walkover means a player advances without playing because the opponent withdrew before the match. A retirement is when a player stops partway through a match, usually through injury or illness, and the opponent wins. A bye is a free pass through a round with no opponent, often given to top seeds when the draw isn't full. A default is a disqualification, for example for serious misconduct.
next: What are seeds and wildcards?
How do tennis rankings work?
What are the Grand Slams?

topics.covers: The visitor asks about national team competitions in tennis, such as the Davis Cup and the Billie Jean King Cup, or about tennis at the Olympics.
topics.answer: The Davis Cup is the men's international team competition, with countries playing each other in a mix of singles and doubles. The Billie Jean King Cup, formerly the Fed Cup, is the women's equivalent. Tennis is also an Olympic sport, with medals in singles, doubles and mixed doubles.
next: What are the ATP and WTA?
What is a calendar Grand Slam?
What are the Grand Slams?

topics.covers: The visitor asks who calls the lines at professional matches, what the chair umpire and line judges do, or how Hawk-Eye and player challenges work.
topics.answer: At pro matches the chair umpire runs the match, announces the score and enforces the rules, while line judges or an electronic system call the lines. Many events let players challenge a call, and a ball-tracking system such as Hawk-Eye shows where the ball landed. A growing number of events now use electronic calls for every line, with no line judges.
next: Is a ball on the line in?
What are the Grand Slams?
How should I behave watching a match?

topics.covers: The visitor asks about spectator etiquette at a professional tournament or stadium match: when to clap, staying quiet, or when you can move to or from your seat.
topics.answer: As a spectator, stay quiet and still during points, and save applause and cheering for when the point ends. At most events you can only leave or take your seat at changeovers, when the players switch ends. Silence your phone, avoid flash photos, and don't cheer a player's double faults or errors.
next: What are the Grand Slams?
How do challenges work?
When do you change ends?

topics.covers: The visitor asks where tennis came from, the history of the game, or what real tennis is.
topics.answer: Modern tennis, first called lawn tennis, took shape in England in the 1870s, and the first Wimbledon championship was held in 1877. It grew out of a much older indoor game now called real tennis, played in an enclosed court where the ball can come off the walls. Real tennis is still played today at a small number of courts.
next: Why is tennis scored 15, 30, 40?
What does love mean?
Why does Wimbledon make players wear white?

topics.covers: The visitor asks why tennis balls are yellow, or why Wimbledon requires players to wear white.
topics.answer: Tennis balls are yellow mainly because the color is easier to see, especially on television, and the rules allow white or yellow balls. White clothing is a tradition from the game's early days, and Wimbledon still keeps a strict all-white dress code for players. Most other tournaments allow any color, though some clubs keep a whites rule.
next: What are the Grand Slams?
Where did tennis come from?
What does love mean?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how tennis compares with pickleball, the differences between them, or which one is easier to learn.
topics.answer: Pickleball is played on a much smaller court, 20 by 44 feet, with a solid paddle and a light plastic ball full of holes. Serves are underhand, there's a no-volley zone near the net called the kitchen, and games usually go to 11. It's quicker to pick up than tennis, while tennis asks more of your movement, footwork and stroke technique, and many people enjoy both.
next: How is padel different from tennis?
How is badminton different from tennis?
Do you teach beginners?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what padel is or how it differs from tennis.
topics.answer: Padel is a racket sport played almost always as doubles, on a smaller court of 20 by 10 meters enclosed by glass and mesh walls. Players use a solid, perforated paddle, serve underhand, and can play the ball off the walls after it bounces. Scoring works the same way as tennis, with 15, 30, 40 and sets.
next: How is pickleball different from tennis?
How is squash different from tennis?
Why is tennis scored 15, 30, 40?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what squash is or how it compares with tennis.
topics.answer: Squash is played indoors in a closed room, where both players share the space and hit a small, hollow rubber ball against the front wall, with no net between them. The ball can come off the side and back walls, and rallies are fast and close. Games are usually played to 11, with a point scored on every rally.
next: How is badminton different from tennis?
How is padel different from tennis?
How is pickleball different from tennis?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how badminton compares with tennis.
topics.answer: Badminton uses a light racket and a feathered or plastic shuttlecock, which must be hit before it touches the ground, so nothing ever bounces. The net is higher than a tennis net, at about five feet, and the court is much smaller. A point is scored on every rally, and matches are usually best of three games.

How is pickleball different from tennis?
What is padel?

topics.covers: The visitor asks why players hit cross-court, or whether cross-court or down the line is the safer default shot in a baseline rally.
topics.answer: Cross-court is the safer default in a rally. The net is lower in the middle than at the sides, the court is longer on the diagonal so you have more room, and you stay closer to the center for the next ball. Most points at every level are built on deep cross-court rallies until someone gets a ball they can attack.
next: When should I hit down the line?
When should I go for a winner?
Where should I stand after I hit?

topics.covers: The visitor asks when to change direction and hit down the line, or why their down-the-line shots keep missing.
topics.answer: Go down the line when you get a ball you can control: not too fast, at a comfortable height, and ideally a bit short. The shot crosses the higher part of the net and has less court to land in, and it leaves you farther from the middle, so hit it with purpose and recover quickly. From a deep, hard ball, cross-court is usually the better choice.
next: Why hit cross-court?
What do I do with a short ball?
Where should I stand after I hit?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether to go for winners or play safe, when to attack, or how aggressive to be during a point.
topics.answer: Play safe until the ball gives you a reason to attack. Stay patient with deep balls, and attack the ones that land short, sit up at a comfortable height, or catch your opponent out of position. Most recreational points end with an error rather than a winner, so making one more ball is often the best tactic. When you do attack, aim a few feet inside the lines.
next: What do I do with a short ball?
How do I beat a pusher?
Why hit cross-court?

topics.covers: The visitor asks where to aim or how to attack a short, sitting ball from the opponent, or which target to pick from inside the baseline. Tactics, not the footwork or swing (ground_short_ball).
topics.answer: Move in, hit it early, and aim deep to a corner, usually your opponent's weaker side, rather than trying to hit the lines. A deep attacking shot pushes them back and often brings a weak reply that you can finish with the next ball. Many players overhit short balls because they look easy, so pick a target with some margin and let your court position do the work.
next: When should I hit a drop shot?
How do I find my opponent's weakness?
When should I go for a winner?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to beat a pusher: an opponent who gets everything back with slow, high or safe shots and waits for them to make errors.
topics.answer: To beat a pusher, accept long rallies and don't try to end the point too early. Hit deep with margin, and when you get a short ball, move in and finish at the net, where their soft, high balls are easy to volley. Drop shots help too, because pushers usually like staying back. Losing to a pusher usually means you're making the errors, so count yours and cut out the risky shots.
next: How do I play a big hitter?
When should I hit a drop shot?
When should I go for a winner?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to play against an opponent who hits groundstrokes very hard, with lots of pace, in rallies.
topics.answer: Against a big hitter, make them hit lots of balls and give them nothing comfortable. Stand a step farther back, use short, compact swings to redirect their pace, and send the ball deep through the middle so they have fewer angles. Low slices and high, deep balls both break their rhythm, because most hard hitters like the ball around waist height. If you keep the ball in play, their errors will come.
next: How do I beat a pusher?
Is it okay to hit down the middle?
What do I do when I'm on defense?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to play against a left-handed opponent, or why lefties feel awkward to play against.
topics.answer: Against a lefty, remember that everything is mirrored. If you're right-handed, your cross-court forehand goes to their backhand, which is often a good pattern, while their cross-court forehand comes to your backhand. Watch for the lefty slice serve on the ad side, the left half of the court as you face the net: it swings wide to a right-hander's backhand, so stand a little wider there. Use the warm-up to get used to their angles.
next: How do I find my opponent's weakness?
How do I play a big hitter?
Why hit cross-court?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to find or figure out an opponent's weakness, or what to watch for during the warm-up and the first few games.
topics.answer: Use the warm-up and the first few games to test them. Hit to both sides, give them a high ball, a low slice and a short ball, and see which ones cause trouble, and notice whether they look comfortable at the net and on overheads. Most players have a weaker side, often the backhand. Once you find it, play there on the important points, but not on every ball, or they'll settle into a rhythm.
next: How do I hide my own weakness?
What if my game plan isn't working?
How do I play against a lefty?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to hide or protect their own weak shot during a match, such as running around a weak backhand.
topics.answer: Protect a weak side by standing slightly toward it, so more balls come to your stronger shot, and run around the ball when you have time. When you can't avoid the weak side, play a safe, high cross-court ball or a deep slice instead of going for too much. Hitting to your opponent's weak side also means fewer good balls come back to yours. Away from matches, keep practising the weak shot.
next: How do I find my opponent's weakness?
My backhand is weak

topics.covers: The visitor asks why hitting deep matters tactically, or how deep to aim in a rally. Why depth matters, not fixing groundstrokes that keep landing short (ground_depth).
topics.answer: Deep balls are the foundation of good tactics, because they push your opponent back and give you more time. A ball landing near the service line lets them step in and attack, while one landing a few feet from the baseline keeps them on defense. To get depth without missing long, aim higher over the net rather than hitting harder, and use topspin to bring the ball down. Aim for the back third of the court, not the line.
next: Is it okay to hit down the middle?
What do I do when I'm on defense?
My forehand flies long

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether it's okay or smart to hit down the middle of the court instead of always aiming for the corners.
topics.answer: Yes, deep down the middle is a smart, safe shot, especially when you're under pressure. It takes away the angles your opponent can use, so they can't easily run you side to side, and it gives you the most room for error. In doubles, the middle also causes confusion over who should take the ball. Save the corners for balls you can control, and use the middle whenever you're unsure.
next: Why hit cross-court?
