topics.covers: The visitor asks how and when to use sharp angles or a short cross-court shot to pull the opponent wide and open up the court.
topics.answer: Use an angle to pull your opponent off the court, then hit the next ball into the space they left. The best time is when you get a comfortable ball that is already wide or a bit short, since a sharp angle from the middle of the baseline is hard to hit. Topspin helps, because it dips the ball down short and wide. A short angle followed by a deep ball to the other side is a classic pattern.
next: When should I hit down the line?
Where should I stand after I hit?
What do I do with a short ball?

topics.covers: The visitor asks where to stand or recover to between shots in a singles rally, or whether to always go back to the center mark.
topics.answer: Recover to the middle of your opponent's possible shots, which isn't always the center mark. After a cross-court shot, you usually don't need to get all the way back: a spot just short of the center, on the side you hit from, covers both of their options. After a down-the-line shot, you have farther to go, to the center or a little past it. Wherever you are, split-step as they hit.
next: Why hit cross-court?
When should I hit down the line?
How do I use angles?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what to do when they're losing a match and their game plan isn't working, or when to change tactics mid-match.
topics.answer: If you're losing and it isn't close, change something. Try a different pattern, such as more balls to their backhand, more height and spin, more slice, coming to the net, or staying back more, and give each change a few games before judging it. If you're winning, keep doing what works. A common saying puts it simply: never change a winning game, always change a losing one.
next: How do I find my opponent's weakness?
How do I beat a pusher?
How should I play the big points?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what to do with the first shot after their serve, the serve plus one, or how to plan the serve and the next ball together.
topics.answer: Plan the serve and the next shot together, a pattern often called the serve plus one. A wide serve tends to open the court, so look to hit the next ball into the open side. A serve to the body or the T often brings a reply to the middle, where you can step around and hit your stronger shot, usually the forehand. After serving, split-step and get ready right away rather than watching the serve.
next: Where should I aim my serve?
How do I use angles?
When should I go for a winner?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to play defense in a rally, how to turn defense back into a neutral rally, or how to get back into a point when the opponent is in control. Hitting a ball while stretched wide is ground_on_the_run.
topics.answer: When you're stretched or pulled wide, buy time instead of going for a winner. Hit high and deep, cross-court or through the middle, or use a low slice, so you have time to get back into position. A high, deep lob works well when your opponent is at the net. The goal on defense is to bring the point back to neutral, then attack again once you're balanced.
next: Is it okay to hit down the middle?
Where should I stand after I hit?
How do I play against someone who rushes the net?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to play against an opponent who comes to the net a lot, or how to stop someone from rushing the net. A match plan, not passing-shot or lob technique (ground_passing_shot, ground_lob).
topics.answer: Against a net rusher, aim low at their feet or lob, and don't feel you must hit a clean winner past them. A dipping ball at their feet forces them to volley up, which often sets up an easy pass on the next shot. Mix in lobs, especially over their backhand side, so they can't crowd the net. Keep your rally balls deep too, because a short ball invites them to come in.
next: What do I do when I'm on defense?
Why should I hit deep?
How do I beat a pusher?

topics.covers: The visitor asks when to use a drop shot in a match, or why their drop shots keep getting run down.
topics.answer: Use the drop shot when your opponent is well behind the baseline and you're inside it, ideally on a short, comfortable ball. It works best against players who stay back or move slowly, and less well against fast movers. Disguise matters, so set up as if you're hitting a normal shot. Drop shots hit from behind your own baseline travel too far and give the other player time to reach them.
next: How do I beat a pusher?
What do I do with a short ball?
How do I use angles?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to play big points tactically, such as break points, 30-40 or game points, or how the score should change how much risk they take.
topics.answer: On big points, raise your margin, not your risk. Get the first serve in, even if it's a bit slower, and make your opponent hit one more ball, because pressure causes errors on both sides of the net. Your highest-percentage pattern, often deep cross-court to their weaker side, is the best choice. When you're well ahead, like 40-0, that's the time to try a riskier shot or something new.
next: Where should I aim my serve?
What if my game plan isn't working?
When should I go for a winner?

topics.covers: The visitor asks for basic doubles tactics: where to aim the ball in doubles, how doubles points are won, or how doubles strategy differs from singles.
topics.answer: In doubles, the team that controls the net usually wins the point, so get both players forward when you can. Keep the ball low and cross-court, away from the opposing net player, aim at their feet when they're up, and use the middle, which causes confusion. Lob when both opponents crowd the net. Doubles rewards good position and teamwork more than big shots.
next: How does one up one back work?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how the one up, one back doubles formation works, or what the baseline player and the net player each do in it.
topics.answer: In one up, one back, one player stays at the baseline while the partner stands at the net, roughly in the middle of their service box. The back player rallies cross-court with the other back player, keeping the ball away from the opposing net player, while the net player watches for balls to intercept. It's the most common formation in social doubles. Its weak spot is the diagonal gap between you, so look for chances to move forward together.
next: When should both of us be at the net?
How do I poach?

topics.covers: The visitor asks when both doubles partners should be at the net, how to play two up, or how to move together as a team at the net.
topics.answer: Both at the net is the strongest doubles position, because you can volley down at sharp angles and cover the court well. Move together as if tied by a rope: when the ball goes to one side, you both shift that way and keep the middle covered. Get there by following a good serve, return or approach, not a weak one. Don't crowd the net: stay about halfway between the service line and the net, so you can still reach lobs.
next: What do we do when they lob over us?
When should we both stay back?

topics.covers: The visitor asks when a doubles team should both stay back on the baseline, or whether two back is a good doubles formation.
topics.answer: Both back is a defensive formation, useful when the other team is volleying well, their net player keeps picking off your returns, or you're facing strong serves. It gives you more time and makes lobs less of a threat. The trade-off is that it's hard to win points from there, so use deep balls and lobs to push the other team back, and move forward together when you get a short ball.

What do we do when they lob over us?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what the I-formation is in doubles, how it works, or how the server and net player use signals in it.
topics.answer: In the I-formation, the server's partner crouches low near the center line at the net, and the server serves from close to the center mark. Before the point, the net player signals which way they'll move, usually with a hand behind the back, and the server covers the other side after serving. The aim is to confuse the returner and stop them settling into a cross-court groove. Practise it before trying it in a match.

topics.covers: The visitor asks what the Australian or tandem formation is in doubles, or when to use it.
topics.answer: In the Australian formation, also called tandem, the server's partner stands at the net on the same side as the server instead of the opposite side. This blocks the returner's usual cross-court return and forces them to go down the line. Use it when a returner keeps hurting you with a strong cross-court return. After serving, the server moves across to cover the open side of the court.
next: What is the I-formation in doubles?
How does one up one back work?
How should I serve in doubles?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how or when to poach in doubles: the timing of moving across, where to hit the poach volley, and how the partner covers the open side.
topics.answer: To poach, move across just as the returner commits to their swing, not earlier, so they can't change direction. Move diagonally forward toward the net rather than sideways, and volley at the feet of the opposing net player or through the gap between them. Once you go, commit fully, and your partner switches to cover the side you left. Even the occasional poach makes returners nervous about the middle.
next: How should we communicate in doubles?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how doubles partners should talk or communicate: calling mine, yours or switch, talking between points, or using hand signals.
topics.answer: Talk early and keep it short. Call mine, yours or switch the moment you know, since a late call can cause more trouble than none. Between points, take a few seconds to agree on a plan, like where the serve is going or whether the net player will poach, and use hand signals if you like. Stay positive with your partner after mistakes, because doubles goes much better when both of you feel supported.
next: Who takes the ball down the middle in doubles?
What is the I-formation in doubles?
How do I poach?

topics.covers: The visitor asks who should take a ball hit down the middle between doubles partners, or how to stop both going for it or both leaving it.
topics.answer: Agree on a rule before you play. A common one is that the player diagonally across from the hitter takes the middle ball, because they have the better angle on it. If you're both at the same depth, the forehand can take it, and if one of you is at the net, the net player takes anything they can reach. Whatever rule you choose, call the ball early.
next: How should we communicate in doubles?
When should both of us be at the net?
What's the basic strategy in doubles?

topics.covers: The visitor asks what to do when opponents lob over the net player in doubles, how switching sides works, or when to use the lob in doubles.
topics.answer: When a lob goes over the net player, the back player usually runs across to chase it and calls switch, and the net player moves over to the other side. If you're both at the net, the player with the better angle or stronger overhead takes it, and you both retreat if neither can. The lob is a weapon for you too: use it over the opposing net player, especially when both opponents crowd the net.
next: When should both of us be at the net?

When should we both stay back?

topics.covers: The visitor asks where the returner's partner should stand in doubles, or what their job is while their partner returns serve.
topics.answer: The returner's partner usually stands around the service line on their side, facing the opposing net player. Their first job is to watch that net player: if the return gets past them, move forward toward the net, and if the return is weak or gets picked off, back up and defend. In casual play they often call the service line too, since they have a good view of it.
next: Where should I aim my return in doubles?

topics.covers: The visitor asks where to aim the return of serve in doubles, or how to keep returns away from the server's partner at the net.
topics.answer: In doubles, the main target is low and cross-court back to the server, away from the net player. If the server follows the serve in, aim low at their feet. Now and then, lob over the net player or go down the line into the alley, which stops them from poaching freely. Consistency matters more than pace: a return that gets past the net player and lands in is a good return.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to serve in doubles, where to stand when serving in doubles, or why first-serve percentage matters more in doubles.
topics.answer: In doubles, a reliable first serve matters more than a fast one, because a weak second serve lets the returner attack your partner at the net. Stand wider than in singles, about halfway between the center mark and the sideline, since you only need to cover your half of the court. Serves to the T or the body tend to bring returns through the middle, where your partner can poach. Agree on the target with your partner first.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how long it takes to learn tennis or get good at it, or how quickly they can expect to improve.
topics.answer: It depends on how often you play, but steady progress is normal. Many beginners who play a couple of times a week can rally and play simple points within a few months, while a reliable serve and solid match skills usually take a year or more of regular play. Progress isn't a straight line, so expect quick jumps and slower stretches. Playing often with a clear focus speeds it up more than anything.
next: How often should I play?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how often they should play or practise tennis each week to improve, or whether playing once a week is enough (not how often to take lessons).
topics.answer: Two or three times a week is a good target for steady improvement. Once a week is enough to enjoy the game and improve slowly, but part of each session goes into finding your timing again. Shorter, more frequent sessions beat one long one, and a rest day between hard sessions helps your body recover. If you can only get on court once a week, add some wall or shadow practice at home.

topics.covers: The visitor asks if they are too old to start tennis or learn it as an adult, such as starting in their 30s, 40s, 50s or later.
topics.answer: No, it's never too late, and many people start tennis as adults and play for decades. Adults often learn quickly because they understand instructions and can practise with purpose. Build sound technique early, since it protects your body and makes the game easier, warm up before you play, and go at a pace that suits your fitness. Doubles is a great way to play socially while you're learning.
next: How long does it take to get good?
What should beginners learn first?
Do you teach beginners?

topics.covers: The visitor feels stuck at the same level, has stopped improving, or keeps losing to the same people despite playing a lot.
topics.answer: A plateau usually means you're playing the same way against the same people. Pick one specific thing to change, such as a weak shot, your second serve or your movement, and practise it on purpose rather than just playing more. Play different opponents, including some a bit better than you, and film yourself to see what's really happening. Sometimes a few lessons are the quickest way to spot what's holding you back.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to use a ball machine, whether a ball machine is worth getting, or how to practise with one.
topics.answer: A ball machine is great for repetition, as long as you practise with a purpose. Start slow with a steady rhythm, work on one shot or one target at a time, and recover to the ready position after each ball instead of standing still. Add movement settings once the stroke feels solid. It can't replace live rallies, because real opponents vary pace and spin, so use it alongside playing with people.

topics.covers: The visitor asks for drills to do with a friend or practice partner, or what two people should practise together on court.
topics.answer: A few simple drills cover most of the game. Rally cross-court forehand to forehand, then backhand to backhand, counting how many you make in a row. Have one player volley at the net while the other hits from the baseline, then swap. Finish by taking turns serving and returning, then play some points. Keeping score in every drill keeps you both focused.

topics.covers: The visitor asks what mini tennis is, or why players rally inside the service boxes before hitting from the baseline.
topics.answer: Mini tennis is rallying gently inside the service boxes, with both players standing near the service line. It's a common way to start a session because it warms up your timing, footwork and touch without full swings. Use soft, short strokes with a little topspin or slice, and try to keep a long rally going. After a few minutes, move back to the baseline.
next: What drills can I do with a friend?
How do I structure a practice session?

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to structure or plan a practice session with a partner, or what to do with an hour on court.
topics.answer: A good hour has a simple shape. Spend about ten minutes warming up with mini tennis and easy rallies, then twenty to thirty minutes on one focus, such as cross-court backhands or second serves. Use the rest to play points or games that test that focus under pressure. One clear focus per session works better than trying to fix everything at once, and ending with points keeps practice close to real matches.
next: What drills can I do with a friend?

Should I use targets when I practise?

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether to use targets or cones in practice, or how to measure their accuracy and depth.
topics.answer: Yes, targets make practice more honest. Put a cone, towel or empty ball can in the court and count how many of ten balls land near it, or mark a zone a few feet inside the baseline to practise depth. Start with big targets and shrink them as you improve. Writing your scores down lets you see real progress over a few weeks instead of guessing.

topics.covers: The visitor asks about filming or recording themselves playing tennis, or how to use their own video to improve.
topics.answer: Filming yourself is one of the quickest ways to improve, because what you feel and what you actually do are often different. Prop your phone up behind the baseline or level with you at the side fence, record a few minutes of rallying or serving, and watch it in slow motion. Look for one thing at a time, such as your contact point or your toss. Film again a few weeks later to compare.

topics.covers: The visitor asks what an NTRP rating is, what numbers like 3.0 or 3.5 mean, or how to get an NTRP rating.
topics.answer: NTRP is the USTA's rating system for adult players, running from 1.5 for a new player to 7.0 for world-class players, in half-point steps. Most recreational players fall somewhere between about 2.5 and 4.5. You can start by rating yourself using the USTA's level descriptions, and if you play USTA league matches, your rating is adjusted based on your results. It's mainly used to place players in fair league matches.

topics.covers: The visitor asks what UTR (Universal Tennis Rating) is, how it is calculated, or what UTR numbers mean.
topics.answer: UTR stands for Universal Tennis Rating, a single scale from 1 to 16.5 used for players of every age and gender. It's calculated from your recent match results, including the scores and your opponents' ratings, so a close loss to a strong player can still help. It's widely used in junior and college tennis and for finding evenly matched opponents. You need recorded match results, such as from tournaments, to get one.
next: What is NTRP?
Do college coaches look at UTR?

topics.covers: The visitor asks about the difference between NTRP and UTR, which rating matters more, or how the two ratings compare.
topics.answer: NTRP is mainly used for USTA adult leagues in the United States, on a short scale from 1.5 to 7.0. UTR is a longer scale from 1 to 16.5, built from match results, and it's popular in junior and college tennis and many events. Which one matters depends on where you play: league players usually care about NTRP, and juniors more often about UTR. There's no exact conversion between them.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to tell whether they are a beginner, intermediate or advanced player, or how to judge their own level.
topics.answer: A rough guide: beginners are learning the strokes and working toward steady rallies and getting serves in. Intermediate players can rally consistently at moderate pace, serve reliably, and play full matches with some direction and spin. Advanced players control pace, spin and placement on most shots, have a dependable second serve, and use tactics under pressure. Ratings like NTRP put numbers on these levels.

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether playing with better or stronger players helps them improve, or how to get better players to hit with them.
topics.answer: Playing better players helps, because you face more pace and spin and learn quickly what works. Mix it with players at your own level, though, where you can try new things and win some points. To get stronger players to hit with you, be reliable: keep the ball in play, warm them up well, and offer to do the drills they want. A hitting partner session is another way to get rallies at a higher level.

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether playing with weaker or lower-level players hurts their game, or how to make those sessions useful.
topics.answer: Playing weaker players doesn't hurt your game if you give yourself a job. Work on consistency, placement and shots you don't trust yet, like slice, volleys or a new serve, since you'll have time to try them. Keep the ball at a pace your partner can return so the rallies last. Being a generous practice partner also makes other players glad to hit with you.

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether tennis lessons are worth it, or whether they should just play more and figure it out themselves.
topics.answer: Both help, and they work best together. Playing builds timing, feel and match experience, but it also repeats whatever habits you already have. Lessons give you feedback on what to change and a plan to practise between sessions. Even a few lessons early on can save you from building habits that are hard to fix later.

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether they can teach themselves tennis, or learn from YouTube and other online videos.
topics.answer: You can learn a lot from videos, especially ideas about grips, footwork and tactics. The hard part is knowing whether you're really doing what the video shows, because many players feel they're doing it when they aren't. Film yourself and compare, work on one idea at a time, and be careful about copying pro strokes exactly, since they're built on years of training, strength and timing.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to fix or unlearn a bad habit in their technique, or how long a technique change takes to stick.
topics.answer: Unlearning a bad habit usually takes a few weeks of steady practice, so fix one habit at a time and start slowly. Practise the new movement with easy balls or shadow swings, and exaggerate it at first, since a change that feels huge often looks small. Expect the old habit to come back under pressure before the new one sticks. Lots of short, focused repetitions work better than one long session.

topics.covers: The visitor says their game got worse after changing a grip, stroke or technique, or wonders whether to switch back to the old way.
topics.answer: A dip after a technique change is normal and usually temporary. Your old stroke was automatic and the new one isn't yet, so you'll miss more for a while, especially in matches. Give it a few weeks of steady practice before judging, and keep working on the change in drills even if you fall back on old habits in matches at first. If it still feels wrong after that, have someone check that the change suits you.

topics.covers: The visitor asks what a tennis beginner should learn first, or in what order to learn the different strokes.
topics.answer: Start with the ready position, the forehand and the backhand, aiming for steady, gentle rallies. Add a simple serve early so you can play real points, and learn basic volleys soon after. Footwork ties it all together: a small hop called the split step as your opponent hits, then moving to the ball before you swing. Spin, power and advanced shots come once you can rally consistently.

topics.covers: A parent asks in general at what age a child can or should start tennis, or whether their child is too young or too old to start.
topics.answer: Children can start tennis whenever they're interested, and many begin around four to six with short courts, small rackets and slower red balls. Young kids learn best through games, so focus on fun and coordination rather than perfect strokes. Kids and teens who start later can still do very well, because tennis rewards practice and athleticism whenever you begin.

topics.covers: A parent asks when their child is ready to start playing tournaments or competitive junior matches.
topics.answer: A child is usually ready for a first tournament when they can serve, rally, keep score and play by the rules without help, and when they actually want to compete. Start with local beginner or entry-level events, which in many areas include red, orange and green ball events for younger players. Treat the first few as learning experiences, and praise effort and fair play more than results.

topics.covers: A parent asks how many hours a week a junior should practise tennis, or how to avoid burnout in a young player.
topics.answer: It depends on age and goals, but enjoyment should set the pace. Younger kids do well with a few short sessions a week plus free play, and hours can grow gradually as a child gets older and more committed. Watch for signs of burnout, like dreading practice, constant tiredness or losing interest, and build in rest and time off. A child who loves the game will keep playing far longer.

topics.covers: A parent asks whether their child should specialize in tennis early or keep playing other sports as well.
topics.answer: For most young kids, playing other sports alongside tennis is a good idea. Many coaches and sports medicine groups advise against specializing too early, because a mix of sports builds all-round athleticism, coordination and enjoyment, and spreads the load on growing bodies. Soccer, basketball and swimming all help tennis footwork and fitness. Tennis can become the main focus later, as the child chooses.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to play college tennis, how to get recruited, or what college coaches look for in junior players.
topics.answer: College coaches generally look at your UTR, tournament results, grades, and how you compete and behave on court. Start by researching schools at a level that fits your rating, then email coaches with your results, academic information and a short match video. The level varies a lot between divisions and schools, so there's often a good fit for players at many levels. Strong grades open more doors.

topics.covers: A parent asks how to support their child's tennis in general: keeping pressure low, valuing effort over results, and leaving the coaching to the coach. Behaving as a spectator is courts_spectating; a child upset after losing is mental_kid_upset.
topics.answer: Support effort and attitude more than results. Before a match, keep things light; during it, cheer good effort quietly and leave the coaching to the coach; afterward, let your child talk first and avoid replaying their mistakes. Asking what they enjoyed or learned works better than asking whether they won. Kids keep playing when tennis feels like theirs, not something they do for you.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to track their tennis progress over time, keep a practice journal, or measure improvement over weeks. Choosing process or outcome goals for a match or season is mental_goals.
topics.answer: Keep a short practice journal: after each session, write what you worked on, how it went and one number, like how many of ten second serves you made. Pick one or two goals you control for the next month, rather than only goals about winning. Over a few weeks, the notes show your real progress and tell you what to work on next.

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether playing doubles helps their singles game or their overall improvement.
topics.answer: Yes, doubles helps your overall game, especially your volleys, returns, serve placement and quick reactions at the net. It also teaches you to hit with control into smaller spaces. You get less baseline rallying and movement than in singles, though, so if singles is your main goal, play both. Many players also find doubles more social, which keeps them on court more often.

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether to spend their court time playing matches and points or doing drills, or how to balance the two.
topics.answer: Do both, because they build different things. Drills give you many repetitions of one shot so it becomes reliable, while matches teach you to choose shots, handle pressure and compete. A good balance is more drilling while you're changing something and more points once it's working. If you only ever play matches, try starting each session with fifteen minutes of focused drills.

topics.covers: The visitor asks how to feed or toss balls to a friend, partner or child so they can practise their strokes.
topics.answer: For beginners, stand a few steps in front of them and off to one side, and toss the ball underhand so it bounces once and reaches them at about waist height. For stronger players, feed from across the net with an easy racket hit, aiming at the same spot each time with a steady rhythm. Keep several balls in your hand or a basket so the drill flows. Consistent feeds make learning much easier for the hitter.

topics.covers: The visitor is returning to tennis after years away or a long break and asks how to get back into the game.
topics.answer: Ease back in rather than playing full matches straight away. Start with a few relaxed hitting sessions to find your timing, warm up properly, and keep your first sessions short so your body can adjust. Your strokes usually come back faster than your fitness and footwork, so focus on moving well. Check your racket too, since strings lose their life over time even when the racket sits unused.

topics.covers: The visitor asks for fun practice games to play with friends or a group, such as cross-court only games or king of the court.
topics.answer: Practice games add pressure and keep sessions fun. Play cross-court only, where any ball outside the diagonal half of the court loses the point, or play to eleven starting each point with a feed instead of a serve. With a group, try king of the court, where the winners stay on one side and challengers rotate in. Tiebreaks with second serves only are great for building a reliable second serve.

topics.covers: The visitor asks whether watching or copying professional players helps them improve their own game, or what to watch for.
topics.answer: Watching pros helps, as long as you watch the right things. Notice their footwork, balance, split step and how early they turn, and how they build points, not only the swing. Their strokes are built for huge pace and years of training, so copy the principles rather than every detail. Watching good club players can be just as useful, because their patterns are closer to yours.
